events.text: The first snow on the north pass, and in it a tiger's prints as wide as a winnowing basket. A charcoal burner did not come home from his kiln. They found his straw sandals, one of them. Now the village shuts its gate at dusk and the dogs whine all night. You are longer than an ox these days, and two lumps on your brow itch like spring shoots. You are not as big as that tiger. Somewhere above you, in the Horn of the east, a star is waiting to see what you do about it.

choices.text: Follow the prints up the pass, alone

ok.log: The prints lead to a cave under a split rock that smells of old blood and wet fur. You learn three things: it is old, it favours its left forepaw, and it hunts at the hour of the ox. You go home with your heart going like a drum.

fail.log: The snow fills the trail by noon. Something on the ridge watches you all the way down. You never see it. You feel it on the back of your neck the whole way. (-8 health)

choices.text: Lie in the frozen paddy and wait for it to move on

effects.log: It does not move on. A tiger that has learned people are easy does not unlearn it. In the night you hear it walk the length of the village wall, sniffing at the gate, and you lie very still and dislike yourself a little.

choices.text: Slap the water every night at the hour of the ox, so the dogs bark and nobody sleeps unguarded

effects.log: Every night you set the dogs off. The village sleeps badly and lives. The headman leaves a bowl of rice on the paddy dyke, for whatever spirit keeps barking the dogs awake.

events.text: Three tiger hunters come up from the county town with spears, a horn bow and a sack of rice the village had to pay for. The court pays hunters by the size of the tiger and by who strikes it first, and these three have done the sums. Two of them spend three days at the headman's table and leave, announcing that the tiger has gone over the mountain. The youngest, {npc}, stays. Seventeen, a borrowed spear, and has never seen a tiger outside a painting. {He} sits on your paddy dyke at dusk, sharpening the spear with hands that will not keep still.

choices.text: Lift your head out of the water and let {him} see you

mem.note: showed me its face on the dyke

effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a long time: the horn buds, the whiskers, the green of you. Then {he} puts the spear down and bows. "So I am not the only fool in this valley who means to stay," {he} says.

choices.text: Leave a trail of your shed scales in the snow, up to the cave under the split rock

mem.note: green scales in the snow, leading the way

effects.log: {npc} follows the scales, finds the cave, and comes back pale and very quiet. That night {he} starts sharpening stakes for a pit.

choices.text: Keep out of it. A spear is a spear, and it may point at you next

effects.log: You stay under the ice. {npc} walks the wall alone every night with a torch, too frightened to sleep and too stubborn to leave. You find you are listening for the footsteps.

events.text: It comes at the hour of the ox, over the back wall of the weaver's yard, where a small child has gone out to the privy with a lamp. The lamp goes over. The child screams once and then does not make any sound at all. {npc} is at the far end of the village with a torch and a spear. Nobody is nearer than you. Nobody is bigger than the tiger. The Horn star is the star of going first.

choices.text: Go over the wall first, horns down

ok.log: You hit it in the flank like a falling tree. It is the biggest thing you have ever touched, and it turns and gets its teeth into your neck, and you do not let go. When {npc} arrives with the torch there is a dragon on top of a tiger in the snow and a child in the privy door, unhurt. The tiger goes over the wall with half an ear gone and never comes back. Far above, in the Horn of the east, a star lights and stays lit.

fail.log: It is older than you, and it has done this before. Its teeth find the soft place behind your jaw.
fail.deathCause: a man-eating tiger in a weaver's yard, faced first

choices.text: Roar from the paddy and draw it out onto the ice

ok.log: You did not know you could roar until you do. The tiger leaves the child for the bigger noise and comes out onto the frozen paddy, where it slides and you do not. {npc} puts a spear into its shoulder from the dyke. Between the two of you, it runs. You hurt everywhere, and over the east the Horn star lights. (-10 health)

fail.log: The roar comes out a croak. The tiger looks at you with contempt and goes back to the yard, and the child lives only because {npc} throws a torch from thirty paces. The Horn star stays dark. (-15 health)

choices.text: Stay in the water. It is a tiger

effects.log: {npc} gets there in time, by a thrown torch and a miracle. The child lives. The tiger leaves with its face burnt. You lie under the ice, and the two buds on your brow ache like a reproach.

events.text: Three winters later the tiger comes back, with a long burn across its face. It has learned that this village fights. It has also learned that it can wait. This time it takes the miller's ox out of the stall, and the next night it is sitting on the mill roof, looking down at the house, in no hurry at all. You have had three winters to think about the night you stayed in the water.

choices.text: Go up the mill wall first, before anyone else can

ok.log: You come up the wall in one movement and take it off the roof. You both land in the millrace. You come out of the water; it does not. In the morning the whole village stands on the bank looking at the biggest tiger anyone has ever seen, and at the long green thing coiled beside it, shivering. The Horn star lights, late, but it lights.

fail.log: It has been waiting three years for exactly this.
fail.deathCause: the tiger with the burnt face, on the mill roof

choices.text: Fog the mill and guide the village men up the pass to its cave while it sleeps

ok.log: Nine men with spears and a pit of stakes. It is clever, and it is cautious, and it is a sound plan. The tiger dies in the pit at dawn. The village is saved. The star in the Horn does not light: courage is going first, and you were sensible instead.

fail.log: The fog lifts too early. The tiger sees the men coming and leaves by the ridge. The miller moves to his cousin in the next county. (-10 health)

choices.text: Let the miller move away. Some fights are not yours

effects.log: The miller loads a cart and goes. The mill rots. The tiger moves on in the spring to find another mill. You do not watch the pass that year.

events.text: {npc} comes back up the valley with a scar across one cheek, a proper spear and six young hunters who follow {him} like ducklings. At dusk {he} sits them on your paddy dyke and tells them about the winter of the weaver's yard. Every time {he} tells it, you are bigger, the tiger is bigger, and the child is smaller. {He} keeps glancing at the water as {he} talks, as if to ask whether you mind.

choices.text: Rise slowly behind the young hunters, so the story gets its proof

mem.note: came up behind the young ones

effects.log: Six young hunters fall off a dyke into a paddy. {npc} laughs until {he} has to sit down in the mud with them. After that night, nobody in the county doubts a word of it, and it grows by an ell every year.

choices.text: Stay down. Let it be the hunter's story

effects.log: You let {npc} have the tiger. The young hunters go home believing a seventeen-year-old with a borrowed spear can save a village, which is a better thing for them to believe than that a dragon will.

choices.text: Leave one of your shed horn tips on the dyke where {he} will find it

mem.note: left me a horn tip on the dyke

effects.log: {npc} finds it at dawn: green, hard as jade, the size of a thumb. {He} does not sell it. {He} wears it on a cord for the rest of {his} life, and is buried with it.

events.text: The lumps on your brow have split the skin. Under it something hard and velvet-covered is pushing out, and it itches the way nothing has ever itched: day and night, waking and sleeping, as if spring itself were trying to get out through your skull. You rub them on rocks. You rub them on the dykes. You rub them on every red pine on the east slope until the trunks are bare to the height of an ox.

choices.text: Rub until they bleed. Anything to stop it

effects.log: You scrape the velvet off in strips and bleed green on the snow. It stops itching for exactly one day. The pines on the east slope weep resin all summer. (-6 health)

choices.text: Soak them in the cold spring under the falls

effects.log: The cold numbs them. You lie with your head in the falls for a month, and in the stillness you feel the horns growing the way you feel the moon pulling: slowly, certainly, from somewhere very far away.

choices.text: Bear it. Horns come when they come

effects.log: You bear it. It is the hardest thing you have done so far, and it looks from the outside exactly like doing nothing. A deer watches you twitching on a rock for an hour and goes away unimpressed.

events.text: {npc}, a herb-gatherer from the market town with a bamboo basket and a sharp eye, finds the bare pines on the east slope and the strips of grey-green velvet caught in the bark. {He} sniffs one, tastes it, and goes very still. Then {he} scrapes every strip into a cloth, ties it, and runs. Within the season, the apothecary in town is selling "deer-antler velvet of a most unusual colour" at three times the price, and a merchant's child with a lung fever has sat up in bed.

choices.text: Rub your horns on the same pines, so there is more for {him}

mem.note: more velvet on the pines every spring

effects.log: Every spring there is more velvet on the east slope, and every spring {npc} comes for it, and sick people in the market town get better. People also start to ask {npc} where it comes from. {He} says: the mountain.

choices.text: Rub them only on the cliff across the river from now on

effects.log: {npc} searches the east slope for two springs and finds nothing but ordinary pine. {He} decides it was a dream and goes back to ordinary ginseng, a little poorer and a little sadder.

choices.text: Rise up out of the bracken behind {him}, all ox-length of you

effects.log: {npc} turns, sees you, and sits down hard on the basket. You look at each other. Then, very slowly, {npc} holds out one strip of velvet, as if to give it back. You find you like {him}.

events.text: A stranger in a fine blue robe with a sword across the back visits {npc}'s stall in the market. Sect people do not ask the price of things. This one sets a purse on the counter that would buy the whole street, and asks where the green velvet comes from, and whether whatever it grows on can be caught alive. {npc} comes up the east slope that night and stands among the bare pines for a long time, not looking for velvet.

choices.text: Show yourself, and shake your head once, slowly

mem.note: shook its head at me, in the pines

ok.log: {npc} nods as if a bargain has been struck. The next day the stranger in blue is told the velvet came from a merchant from the far north, now dead. The purse goes back across the counter. {npc} eats plain barley for a year and does not seem to mind.

mem.note: too big, too close, too much

fail.log: {npc} panics at the size of you and runs. In the morning {he} takes the purse. Within a month there are men with nets and iron hooks on the east slope, and you learn what a sect thinks a dragon is for.

choices.text: Move every rubbing-tree you use to the cliffs where nobody can climb

effects.log: The stranger in blue spends a summer on the east slope and finds bare pines and nothing else. {npc} spends the same summer looking at you sideways whenever you pass, which you consider fair.

choices.text: Visit the stranger's inn at night and breathe on the window

effects.log: The stranger in blue wakes to a green eye the size of a bowl at the paper window, and is a sensible person, and leaves for the capital at dawn. Sensible people tell other people, though.

events.text: Your neck has grown long enough that you can lie in the river reeds and see over the barley. So you see it: the headman's son, {npc}, coming out of the widow Kang's threshing shed in the middle of the night where {he} had no business being, knocking over the lamp as {he} goes, and running. The shed burns. So does a whole year of barley and the ox tethered behind it. By noon the village has decided the fire was set by Dolsoe, the hired hand from nowhere, who sleeps in the shed and has nobody to speak up.

choices.text: Watch, and remember every face

effects.log: You remember {npc} running. You remember the headman not asking where {npc} was. You remember Dolsoe, black with soot, trying to drag the ox out by the horns while the roof came down. A dragon's memory is long, and it is not kind.

choices.text: Follow {npc} home and look in at the paper window until {he} sees your eye

effects.log: {npc} sees a green eye the size of a rice bowl at the window and does not sleep for a week. Nobody else in the house sleeps either, because {npc} will not say why.

choices.text: Throw the river at the fire

ok.log: A wave comes out of the river and over the dyke and onto the shed, and half the barley is saved, steaming. The ox is not. Nobody can explain the wave. Everybody can explain the fire, and they explain it wrong.

fail.log: You throw the river and most of it lands in the barley field next door. The shed burns to the ground. (-6 health)

events.text: The county magistrate cannot decide. Dolsoe swears; {npc} swears louder and has a father. So the magistrate does what magistrates in this county have done with hard cases for three hundred years: at dawn the hired hand will be brought to the river, and heaven will judge. If the dragon of the river shows itself, the man is innocent. If the water stays still, the hired hand hangs. That night the old headman comes down to the reeds alone, kneels, and lays out a year of offerings on the bank. "My only son," the old man whispers to the water. "Stay down tomorrow. Only stay down."

choices.text: Nose the offerings back into the reeds

effects.log: The rice cakes float away in the dark. The old headman watches them go and covers the face with both hands and stays kneeling a long time. Then goes home without a lamp.

choices.text: Eat the offerings. You have not promised anything

effects.log: Steamed rice cakes, dried persimmons, a whole boiled chicken. The headman hears you eating in the dark and goes home weak with relief. You have not promised anything. You are aware that the headman thinks you have.

choices.text: Go and look at Dolsoe, tied up in the headman's storehouse

effects.log: Through a crack in the boards you watch the hired hand, who cannot read, practising the one prayer the village mudang taught everyone as children, over and over, getting it slightly wrong every time. The man who set no fire prays all night. Across the yard, {npc}, who did, sleeps.

events.text: Dawn. The whole village on the gravel by the river, the magistrate under a parasol, Dolsoe kneeling with the rope already over the zelkova branch. {npc} stands behind {his} father, white. The river is flat as a mirror. Everyone is looking at it. A dragon cannot yet speak a human word. But staying still, today, would be a word, and so would rising.

choices.text: Rise. All of you, neck first, in front of everyone

effects.log: You come up out of the river and the neck keeps coming, up and up, until your head is higher than the zelkova. Nobody breathes. The magistrate drops the brush. Dolsoe is cut loose, and every face turns to {npc}, who runs, and is caught at the ford. In the Eastern Palace the Neck star lights: the throat that does not lie.

choices.text: Stay down, as the old man begged

effects.log: The water stays flat. At noon the hired hand hangs from the zelkova. {npc} does not come to watch. The Neck star stays dark, and the silence in your throat tastes of iron for a long time after.

choices.text: Rise only as far as your eyes, and look at {npc} alone

ok.log: Two green eyes come up out of the flat water, and they look at nobody but {npc}. {npc} looks back, and breaks, and walks out in front of the whole village and says it: the lamp, the shed, the running. A word you made someone else say is still a true word. The Neck star lights.

fail.log: Only {npc} sees you, and {npc} has had all night to become someone who says nothing. The magistrate sees only still water. The hired hand hangs. Half a truth, it turns out, is just a quieter silence.

events.text: {npc} was flogged and sent to boil salt on the east coast for ten years. Ten years is long. {npc} comes back thin and burnt brown, missing two fingers, walks straight past the family gate and down to the river, and stands on the gravel where the ordeal was. "You could have stayed down," {he} says at last. "Everyone says my father asked you."

choices.text: Rise, and wait

mem.note: came up and waited for me

effects.log: You come up and wait. {npc} waits too. Then {he} nods, very slightly, as if to an equal, and goes to the widow Kang's house and rebuilds the threshing shed with eight fingers, alone, over one autumn. Nobody helps. Nobody stops {him} either.

choices.text: Splash {him}, once, like a child would

mem.note: splashed me

effects.log: {npc} stands there dripping. Then laughs, for the first time in a decade, a rusty sound. "Fair," {he} says.

choices.text: Stay down. A river owes nobody an answer

effects.log: {npc} waits until dark and then goes. The next year {he} is the one who carries Dolsoe's firewood to the market every fifth day. Neither of them ever says why.

events.text: {npc} is headman now. {He} collects the grain levy with a stick, had the zelkova by the river cut down for timber, and every spring holds a rite on the gravel to thank the dragon of the river, who once judged so wisely. There is a table of offerings and a speech. In the speech you are very wise indeed. The stump of the zelkova is still there, at the back, where nobody looks.

choices.text: Rise in the middle of the speech and look only at {npc}

mem.note: looked at me in front of everyone

effects.log: {npc} stops in the middle of a sentence and does not find the end of it. The village goes home uneasy. The rite is held indoors from then on.

choices.text: Rise over the stump of the hanged man's tree, in front of everyone

ok.log: You come up over the stump and stay there, head bowed over it, while the speech dies. Nobody needs it explained. The old women start to weep first; then everyone remembers what they decided not to remember. Late, too late for Dolsoe, the Neck star lights over the east.

fail.log: You rise over the stump and the village bows to you, and to the stump, and decides it is a holy stump. {npc} builds a little shrine on it. You have accidentally become the god of the thing you meant to accuse.

choices.text: Flood {his} paddies, and only {his}

effects.log: One field drowns in a dry spring. {npc} understands, and is frightened, and is crueller to everyone else to make up for it. You have learned something about punishment.

events.text: A travelling scholar sits on your riverbank reading the Book of Changes aloud to himself, for the cool. The first line of the first hexagram: hidden dragon, do not act. You remember that. Then the dragon in the field, then the flying dragon, then the last line: the arrogant dragon will have regret. He looks at the Neck star coming out over the ridge and says to nobody, "Strange. The old astronomers write that star with the very same sign as the arrogant dragon. High. Too high."

choices.text: Dive for a whole season and think about it

effects.log: You lie at the bottom of the deep pool through the autumn, and think about necks, and how high they lift a head, and how far it is to fall from the top of one.

choices.text: Rise higher than you have ever risen, just to see

effects.log: You go up into the night until the river is a thread and the scholar is a dot. It is magnificent. You are magnificent. The scholar, below, has dropped the book in the water. On the way down it occurs to you that you did that to prove a book wrong, which is exactly what the book said you would do.

choices.text: Listen to the rest of the book

effects.log: He reads until the lamp oil runs out: the Earth, the Thunder, the Mountain, the Waiting. You understand perhaps a tenth of it. A tenth is more than most dragons ever bother to.

events.text: The third month with no rain. The rice seedlings in the beds have gone the colour of straw. The village well drops a rope's length a week, and the old women walk to the next valley with jars on their heads and come back with half of what they took. And you, lying in the shrinking pool, can feel it: wet, out over the sea, three days away, a smell like iron and green leaves. You have never pulled a cloud. You suspect you could.

choices.text: Reach for it

ok.log: You reach with something that is not your claws, and far out over the sea a cloud the size of a county leans, very slightly, toward you. It is like pulling a whale with a hair. It is also the most natural thing you have ever done.

fail.log: You reach and nothing reaches back. You lie in the mud with a headache like a split log. (-6 health)

choices.text: Wait. Heaven sends rain when heaven decides

effects.log: You wait. Heaven does not seem to have decided. A child dies of the summer flux in the next village, and you think about the word "decides" for a long time.

choices.text: Carry water from the deep pool in your mouth to the seedbeds, a mouthful at a time

effects.log: All night, every night, a hundred trips. The seedbeds nearest the pool stay green. The farmers find the mud wet each morning and cannot work out why, and leave a bowl of rice on the dyke just in case. (-5 health)

events.text: The drought goes into a fourth month. The magistrate holds a rite on the hill; the village mudang dances; a farmer hangs a prayer on paper from the willow over your pool. You lie under the willow and look at the paper turning in the hot wind. Then you rise out of the pool, all of you, and go up.

choices.text: Pull the whole cloud over the valley

ok.log: It comes over the ridge like a black ox, and you are inside it, and then it breaks. Three days of rain. The paddies drink, the well fills, the old women stand in the lanes with their faces turned up and their mouths open. Somebody saw a green tail in the cloud. By autumn, everybody did.

fail.log: You pull until something tears in your shoulders, and the cloud goes on along the coast and rains on the sea. (-12 health)

choices.text: Call a small rain, only over the seedbeds

effects.log: A grey curtain the width of three fields. The seedbeds stand up. The fields beyond stay brown, but the seed for next year is safe. Nobody sees you. The farmers credit the mudang, who has the decency to look surprised.

choices.text: Go back down. Rain is heaven's, not yours

effects.log: You lie back down under the willow. The rain comes eleven days later, on its own. The harvest is thin, not dead. You do not know if you were wise or a coward, which is, the old scholar on the bank would tell you, the usual condition.

events.text: Heaven keeps accounts. The cloud you pulled was owed somewhere else: a salt-flat that needed the sun, a county to the south, a ledger in the sky you have never seen. On the first night of the new moon a storm comes over the ridge that you did not call, and the lightning in it walks across the valley like a man looking for someone, striking pine after pine, coming closer.

choices.text: Dive to the bottom of the deep pool and let it pass

effects.log: It strikes the pool three times. The water boils over you. Then it goes on east, still looking, and you come up at dawn with your scales scorched and a very clear understanding that heaven noticed. (-10 health)

choices.text: Rise and take the lightning on your horns

ok.log: It hits you on the horns and goes through you and out by the tail into the river, and you are still there, smoking. The whole valley saw. For a moment you feel like the sky. The moment is the dangerous part. (-12 health)

fail.log: It hits you on the horns and you find out what heaven thinks of dragons who argue.
fail.deathCause: heaven's lightning, for rain called without leave

choices.text: Bow your head to the storm

ok.log: You lie flat on the bank with your head down, and the lightning stands over you for a long moment, crackling. Then it goes. Heaven seems to accept an apology. It will not, you suspect, accept a second.

fail.log: Heaven is not in the mood for bowing. A pine falls on you. (-15 health)

events.text: That autumn the village holds a rain-thanks rite at your pool for the first time. Rice cakes in five colours, a pig's head, a jar of rice liquor poured on the water, and the children in clean clothes bowing in a row. The headman reads a long speech to the Dragon King of the Pool. They have given you a title. It is a long title.

choices.text: Take the cakes, and rise a little, so they know

effects.log: The children shriek. The headman faints, briefly, from joy. From now on there is a rite every autumn, and every autumn the title is a little longer. You notice you look forward to it. You notice that you notice.

choices.text: Give next year's first rain to the valley over the ridge that got none

effects.log: The next spring it rains first in the poor valley beyond the ridge, where nobody has ever held a rite for you. They do not know why. They hold one anyway. You go to it and are bored, and feel better than you have all year.

choices.text: Lie deep under the rite until it is over

effects.log: You hear the speech through the water, muffled, like rain on a roof. It is a very good speech. It is about somebody much grander than you.

events.text: The market town down the river has had enough of drought, and the merchants have built dragons: four of them, out of straw and bamboo, green paper for scales, each as long as an ox-cart, set up in the square facing east. In front of them a mudang, {npc}, has been dancing for two days and two nights without sleeping, bells in one hand, a fan in the other, calling the dragons by name. None of the names is yours. You are, however, the only dragon within a hundred li.

choices.text: Answer. Rain on the market, on the drum, on the straw dragons

mem.note: answered my dance

effects.log: The first drop lands on the drum. The drummer stops. {npc} does not. {He} dances on in the rain with the paper scales of the straw dragons running green into the gutters, and by the time it stops {he} is the most famous mudang in the province.

choices.text: Answer, but rain on the fields outside the town, not the square

mem.note: rained, but not on me

effects.log: The fields get the rain. The square stays dusty, and {npc}, still dancing, gets none of the credit. {He} looks up at the clouds going the wrong way and laughs out loud, which is how you know {he} is a real one.

choices.text: Stay above the clouds and watch

effects.log: {npc} dances a third day and a fourth and falls down on the fifth. The rain comes on the sixth, by itself. Everyone agrees the mudang did it. {npc}, lying in bed with feet like raw meat, knows better.

events.text: Another drought, and this time you are far away on the spring wind when the dancing starts. When you come home the polite rite has failed, and the town has turned to the old rude one. At dawn {npc} leads a crowd up to your pool with a dog's carcass on a pole. The idea is very old: foul the dragon's water, and the dragon will be angry enough to wash it clean with rain. {npc} looks unhappy about it. {npc} throws the dog in anyway.

choices.text: Wash it out with rain, as they want

mem.note: washed the pool, as we asked

effects.log: You wash the pool clean with three days of rain, and the town learns that the rude rite works. You will be getting a dead dog in your water every dry year for the next two centuries. You think about that afterwards.

choices.text: Wash it out with a flood, straight onto the market

mem.note: flooded the market

effects.log: The market goes under to the knees. Melons float down the main street. Nobody dies. Nobody fouls the pool again either, and {npc} has a lot of explaining to do.

choices.text: Lie in the filth and refuse

mem.note: would not be bullied

effects.log: You lie in the stink for nine days. The town gives up. The rain comes on the tenth, from the west, from nobody. {npc} comes back alone and drags the dog out with a rake, and sits on the bank afterwards for a while, not dancing. (-6 health)

events.text: A new magistrate has come from the capital, a strict Confucian with a list of things to stamp out, and shamans are at the top. {npc} is arrested in the square, mid-dance, for deceiving the people, and is to be flogged on the fifth day and banished. On the fourth night there is no moon. The magistrate's office has a pond in the courtyard.

choices.text: Rise out of the magistrate's pond at dawn, in full sight of the yamen

mem.note: rose in the magistrate's pond for me

effects.log: The magistrate opens the door to wash and finds a dragon in the courtyard pond, looking at the door. The magistrate shuts it again. {npc} is released at noon "for lack of evidence", and the next shaman to be arrested in that county is arrested about a hundred years later.

choices.text: Rain on the fifth day, all day, so the flogging cannot be held in the square

mem.note: sent a rain that would not stop

effects.log: It rains for nine days. The flogging is postponed, and postponed, and on the tenth day the magistrate, who is not a stupid person, lets {npc} quietly out of the back gate with a warning. {npc} leaves a bowl of rice at your pool every month for the rest of {his} life.

choices.text: Do nothing. Shamans and magistrates have been at this for a thousand years

effects.log: {npc} is flogged and banished to an island in the south. From the island, two years later, comes a story about a mudang who dances on the beach for the fishermen and is never once wrong about the weather. You hope it is the same one.

events.text: {npc} is old now, and has asked to be carried up to your pool to die. The family set the bed on the bank. At dusk the young mudang who took over the rites burns one last straw dragon on the gravel, green paper and all, and the sparks go up into the dark. "Thirty years I told them what you wanted," {npc} says to the water, in an ordinary voice. "I made most of it up. You let me. Thank you."

choices.text: Rise into the sparks, all of you, for {him} alone

effects.npcPass: on the bank of the dragon pool, at dusk, smiling

mem.note: came up in the sparks, at the end

effects.log: You come up through the burning straw dragon and the sparks run along your scales like a second set of stars. {npc} looks for a long time. "Much bigger than I said," {he} says, and laughs, and dies before the laugh is finished.

choices.text: Ring the brass bells on the offering table with the tip of your tail

effects.npcPass: on the bank of the dragon pool, listening to bells

mem.note: rang my bells

effects.log: The bells jingle once, twice, three times. {npc} closes {his} eyes to listen and does not open them again. The young mudang keeps those bells for years and never lets anyone else touch them.

choices.text: Let a soft rain fall on the bank, and nowhere else

effects.npcPass: in a soft rain at the dragon pool
effects.log: It rains on the bed and the gravel and the burning straw and nowhere else. The family put up oiled paper. {npc} pushes it away, and lies with {his} face in the rain, and goes.

events.text: Two palace servants in grey with a cart full of earthenware jars come wading up your stream, turning over stones. They are catching salamanders: as many as they can, for the court. The king is to hold the lizard rite for rain, and the lizards, the court says, are the dragon's little kin. You watch them drop your little kin into the jars one by one and stopper them with straw.

choices.text: Follow the jars to the capital

effects.log: You follow the cart down the river and along the royal road for nine days, travelling at night, in ditches and rice channels and once, regrettably, a fishpond. The capital smells of smoke and ten thousand people. The jars go in through a side gate of the palace.

choices.text: Let the salamanders out of the jars at night

effects.log: In the morning every jar is empty and full of water. The servants look at each other and go and catch more, further downstream, where you cannot follow without being seen. You have saved forty salamanders and doomed forty others. Kinship is complicated.

choices.text: It is a court matter. Stay in the deep

effects.log: The cart creaks off down the valley. You hear later that it rained in the capital, eventually, and that the court was very pleased with itself.

events.text: The palace. A courtyard of hot grey stone, an altar, ministers in red robes sweating under their hats. Twenty children in blue robes, each with a jar and a willow stick, beat the jars and chant: lizard, lizard, raise the clouds, raise the rain, and we will let you go. The sun is merciless. Inside the jars, your kin are cooking. One child, {npc}, nine years old, is only tapping the jar, and whispering into the mouth of it between taps.

choices.text: Rain on the palace, now, all of it

effects.log: You come over the palace roofs in a black cloud and empty it on the courtyard. The ministers flee for the eaves. The children dance. The jars are opened. A court historian writes that heaven answered the king's sincerity, and you, curled in a cloud over the capital, feel very much like a dragon a king has summoned. You are not sure you like it.

choices.text: Rain only on {npc}

mem.note: let rain fall only on me

ok.log: A cloud the size of a courtyard tree drifts over the palace and rains on one small blue robe and its jar and nowhere else. The court is thunderstruck. By evening it has been decided that the child is blessed, and by the next day it rains on everyone, because you have the general idea now.

fail.log: You aim for the child and hit the Minister of Rites, very precisely, all afternoon. The Minister of Rites is declared blessed. {npc} gets no rain at all and is scolded for not beating the jar hard enough.

choices.text: Refuse. A rain bought with beaten jars buys nothing

effects.log: The rite goes on for seven days. On the seventh the lizards are dead in the jars and the child who would not beat {his} jar is caned in front of the others. The rain comes on the ninth day, from the sea, on its own. You go home feeling right, which is not the same thing as good.

events.text: A junior official from the Office of Rites rides up your valley with two clerks and a parasol: {npc}, grown, in the green robe of the seventh rank, with the court's new instructions for the provincial rain rites. When the clerks go to water the horses, {npc} walks down to your stream alone, crouches, and turns over a stone. A salamander looks up. {npc} puts the stone back very gently. "I remember the rain," {he} says to the stream.

choices.text: Let {him} see you in the stream, just your head

mem.note: showed yourself to me in your own stream

effects.log: {npc} does not jump. {He} bows from the crouch, deeply, and says, "I am going to change the rite. It will take me thirty years." Then {he} goes back to the horses and says nothing to the clerks at all.

choices.text: Send a little rain after the parasol all the way back to the capital

mem.note: sent a little cloud to follow me home

effects.log: A small private cloud follows {npc}'s parasol for nine days. The clerks are alarmed. {npc} is delighted, and tells nobody why, and is promoted twice that year for no reason the Office of Rites can work out.

choices.text: Stay hidden. Officials are officials, however they began

effects.log: {npc} waits by the stream until the clerks call, then goes. The new instructions, when the county reads them, say the lizards must be released unharmed after every rite, by order of the Office of Rites. Nobody knows who wrote that line.

events.text: {npc} is Minister of Rites now, old and stooped in a red robe with a crane on the breast, and in the worst drought for forty years {he} holds the lizard rite at court for the last time. Twenty children in blue. Twenty jars. No sticks: the new rule. The children only sing, and at the end of the song, by the minister's order, they open the jars and let the lizards run free across the hot stone, every one.

choices.text: Rain before the last lizard reaches the gutter

mem.note: rained when we let them go

effects.log: The cloud comes over the palace while the lizards are still running, and the children sing it down. {npc} stands in the rain without a parasol, with {his} face turned up, and the court historian, who knows nothing, writes that the minister wept for the people.

choices.text: Rain on the capital, and on every village that ever beat a jar, all on the same day

mem.note: rain on the whole kingdom

ok.log: It rains from the coast to the northern rivers in one day. In every village where children beat lizards in jars, the children stand in the rain and wonder whether they are supposed to beat them harder next time, or not at all. The minister's new rite is copied everywhere within a year.

fail.log: Too much sky, too far. You get rain onto the capital and nowhere else, and lie in a river for a month with your whole body aching. (-14 health)

choices.text: Wait three days, so the new rite is not mistaken for a trick

effects.log: It rains on the third day. The court argues for a month about whether the new rite worked. {npc} does not argue; {he} only smiles, and orders the jars to be made smaller, so they will be easier to open.

events.text: It has ached for ten years, low in each foot, like a stone in a sandal. One spring morning you grip the cliff at the head of the valley and there are four of them: three old claws, dark as wet slate, and a new one, pale as jade, curved like a new moon. Four claws. Old serpents in deep pools say a dragon needs four to hold the wish-pearl. You flex it. It is ridiculous how pleased you are.

choices.text: Score your mark in the cliff with it

effects.log: Four long grooves in the granite at the head of the valley, deep as a finger. For the next thousand years, hunters will put their hands in them and argue about what bear could possibly have made them.

choices.text: Hold something small with it: one pine seed, without crushing it

ok.log: It takes you nine days. On the tenth you hold a pine seed between the new claw and the old and do not crush it, and plant it in a crack in the rock. It is a pine now, crooked and very old. That is what a fourth claw is for.

fail.log: You crush a great many pine seeds. The squirrels of the valley regard this as a declaration of war.

choices.text: Show nobody. Claws are not for showing

effects.log: You fold it under the others and lie down on it. Nobody counts a ridge's claws. Somewhere in the Eastern Palace, someone does.

events.text: A landslide after the spring rains: half the slope above the charcoal-burners' huts begins to go, slowly, with a noise like a tired ox. Three children are in the lowest hut. Your new claw is already moving before you have decided anything.

choices.text: Catch the slope with all four claws and hold it

ok.log: You hold the whole hillside on four claws while the children run, and then you let it down gently into the stream, where it makes a new pool. The charcoal-burners name the pool after the claw. They have no idea it was a claw. They just like the shape.

fail.log: You hold it long enough. The children get out. Then the slope takes your new claw with it and you lie in the mud for a season, waiting for it to grow back, which it does, crooked. (-15 health)

choices.text: Lift the hut, children and all, and set it down on the far bank

effects.log: The children ride out the landslide inside the hut, in the air, screaming with joy. When they tell the story, nobody believes them, which they find unbearable for the rest of their lives.

events.text: You are too long now for any pool. One autumn, at the head of a valley, you lie down along a ridge to rest, and in the spring there are roots in you: pine roots, through the gaps in your scales, gently, the way they go through rock. Above the ridge the third mansion of the Eastern Palace hangs low, the Root star, the star of patience. Its trial is very simple. Lie still. Do not move, whatever happens, for forty years.

choices.text: Lie down, and do not move for forty years

effects.log: You close your eyes. The roots go deeper. Moss starts on your east side within the year. A dragon's first lesson was do not act; it turns out to be the last one too, and every one in between.

choices.text: Walk the whole ridge first, end to end, to know what you are lying on

effects.log: Nine li of ridge, three springs, a fox den, a buried bronze bell from some old war, a spring that tastes of iron. Then you lie down along it like a sleeper in a familiar bed, and begin.

choices.text: Lie down, but keep one eye open

effects.log: One eye, half shut, looking down the valley. You tell yourself it does not count as moving. The Root star, above, does not say whether it agrees.

events.text: Quarrymen. The village needs a new millstone and a wall for the granary, and the granite on the east face of the ridge is the best in the county. All summer they cut at your flank with chisels and wedges and wet wood, and the village argues at night about whether the old women are right, and the ridge really breathes. "Hills do not breathe," says the master mason, and drives the next wedge.

choices.text: Do not move

effects.log: Every wedge is a scale cracking. You do not move. By autumn the village has a fine millstone and a wall, and the master mason has decided the ridge is just a ridge. You lie there with a hole in your side and the Root star burning above. (-8 health)

choices.text: Twitch, once

effects.log: The whole east face shivers like a horse's flank. Three quarrymen fall off a ledge into a bush. The master mason picks up the tools without a word and goes home, and the quarry is never worked again. Above the ridge the Root star flickers.

choices.text: Let the spring under the quarry come up, quietly

ok.log: A spring breaks out of the quarry floor and floods it in a night. The quarrymen give up and build their wall from river stone. The flooded quarry becomes the best swimming hole in the valley. You did not move. Not exactly.

fail.log: To push the spring up you have to shift, and you shift too much. The east face groans. The quarrymen run. The Root star flickers. (-4 health)

events.text: A child of the village, {npc}, has decided the ridge is a person. {He} climbs up every evening and sits on a particular rock that is, in fact, the base of your left horn, and tells you everything: who stole whose persimmons, what the headman said, why the old grandmother next door cries at night. Every evening {he} asks the same question at the end. "Are you really a dragon? If you are, move. Just a little. I will not tell."

choices.text: Do not move. Listen

mem.note: listened to me from the ridge

effects.log: Six years of evenings. {npc} grows up on that rock, telling you the whole village. One evening {he} does not ask the question at the end any more. That is how you know {he} has decided, either way.

choices.text: Move one pine needle, only one

mem.note: moved a needle for me

effects.log: One needle, on one pine, against the wind. {npc} sees it, gasps, and keeps the promise: tells nobody, for years. Above, the Root star flickers. It was worth it. Probably.

choices.text: Breathe a little warm air onto the rock on cold evenings

mem.note: warmed the rock on the ridge for me

ok.log: The rock is always warm, even in winter. {npc} does not know why and decides it does not need to know. Breath is not moving. The Root star does not mind.

fail.log: You breathe too hard and the rock shifts under {npc}, who tumbles off into the bracken, sits up, and stares at the ridge with enormous eyes. The Root star flickers.

events.text: A dry year, then another. The paddies crack. The village mudang declares that the ridge has died, and a dead ridge drinks the valley's water and must be cut: a trench through its neck, to let the bad luck out. The men go up with mattocks. You could rain. You could shake them off. You would have to move.

choices.text: Do not move. Let them dig

effects.log: They dig a trench three spades deep across your neck. It hurts in a way you have no word for. The rain comes by itself a month later, and the village decides the trench worked. You lie still with a wound in your throat and the Root star burning very bright. (-12 health)

choices.text: Rain. A village is worth one movement

effects.log: You turn your head to the sea and pull, and the rain comes in an hour. The men throw down their mattocks and dance in the mud. The trench is never dug. Above, the Root star dims, the way a lamp dims when a door opens.

choices.text: Let the spring in the old quarry run down to the paddies

ok.log: You open the spring from inside, the way you would breathe out, without moving a scale. Water runs down the old quarry channel into the paddies. The mudang declares the ridge has come back to life. The trench is filled in. You did not move.

fail.log: The spring will not come without a push, and you will not push. They dig the trench. (-10 health)

events.text: Forty years. The pines on your back are thick as a farmer's waist. The village children are grandparents. The trench is moss, the quarry is a swimming hole, and nobody living has ever seen the ridge move. One clear night you feel it: the Root star, low over the valley, looks down at you the way you look down at a seed you have planted, and decides.

choices.text: Open your eyes, slowly

effects.log: You open your eyes. Pine needles fall from your lids. Above, the third mansion lights and stays lit: patience, which looks from the outside like nothing at all for years. The valley below feels its ridge wake, has a very good harvest, and does not know why.

choices.text: Lie still one more year, for good measure

effects.log: One more year. It is the easiest year of the forty. When you finally open your eyes the Root star has been lit for a year already, waiting politely for you to notice.

events.text: You moved. Once, for a good reason, perhaps. The Root star does not care about reasons. It hangs over the ridge dim and patient, and you understand that the forty years begin again from the day you stopped being still.

choices.text: Lie down and begin the forty years again

ok.log: The second forty are easier than the first, because you know now how long forty years is. When they end, the Root star lights, and the valley has never known a calmer generation.

fail.log: Twelve years in, a fire starts on the south slope, and you move again before you have decided to. The Root star stays dim. Perhaps patience is not a virtue you can practise twice in the same century.

choices.text: Accept it. You moved for the village, and you would again

effects.log: You get up and shake off forty years of moss. The Root star stays dark this time. Somewhere in the Eastern Palace a seat notes it. In the valley, the paddies are full.

events.text: There are three valleys east of the great river where a dragon of your length could lie down and be a ridge. The first is narrow and stony, with a poor village that works hard and has no water. The second is wide and empty: a mountain at its back, a stream winding across its mouth like a sash, and on the right a ridge of pale rock where something with stripes lives. The third looks down on the market town, where the rich would build in your shelter and pay well for the privilege.

choices.text: The narrow valley. They need the water most

effects.log: You lie down along the north side of the stony valley and turn the snowmelt toward its fields. The first spring there is a stream where there was a ditch. The village has no idea what happened and holds a rite to the mountain spirit, who has no idea either.

choices.text: The wide valley, mountain behind and water in front, with the white ridge opposite

effects.log: Left azure dragon, right white tiger, mountain behind, water in front: the geomancers will call it the perfect site, later, and argue about who found it first. Nobody lives there yet. On the pale ridge opposite, something lifts its head and watches you lie down.

choices.text: Above the market town, where the rich will build

effects.log: Within a few years there are tiled roofs climbing your lower slopes and a family shrine on your shoulder. The rich are very grateful to the hill, in a businesslike way. They put up a stone with your name on it. The name is spelt wrong.

events.text: A geomancer walks your spine in a white robe and a wide black hat, holding a round lacquered compass with nine rings of tiny characters and a needle that will not settle. {npc} has read every book on dragon veins in the province and found the books wrong about half of everything. At the head of the ridge {he} stops, looks down the whole length of you, and says aloud to nobody: "This is not a ridge that looks like a dragon. This is a dragon that is pretending to be a ridge."

choices.text: Let {him} walk your whole length

mem.note: let me walk the whole vein

effects.log: {npc} walks for nine days, writing in a little book: where your heart is, where your breath comes out, where the vein runs closest to the surface. At your tail {he} bows, and then, a little embarrassed, bows again toward your head, nine li away.

choices.text: Turn the needle on the compass, slowly, until it points at {his} nose

mem.note: turned my needle

effects.log: {npc} stares at the compass. Then {he} sits down on your back and laughs until the tears come. "Very well," {he} says. "I will not tell anyone where you are. Just let me have my needle back."

choices.text: Breathe a cold fog along your back until {he} leaves

effects.log: {npc} leaves in the fog, but slowly, taking notes. You have the feeling you have just confirmed something.

events.text: {npc} comes back with two clients, on two different days. The first is a rich family from the capital who want the best site in your embrace for a manor and will pay a fortune. The second is a family of slash-and-burn farmers from the high hills whose fields are worn out, who own a cooking pot, a hoe and four children. {npc} stands at the head of the ridge with the compass in hand, waiting to see which way the needle points.

choices.text: Point the needle at the farmers

mem.note: pointed my needle at the poor

effects.log: The needle swings to the bend in the stream where the farmers are standing and stays there. {npc} tells the rich family the omens are poor this year, and waives the farmers' fee. {He} walks home much poorer and whistling.

choices.text: Point the needle at the rich family

mem.note: pointed my needle at the rich

effects.log: A manor goes up with a tiled roof and a pond. The valley gets a road, a market day, and a landlord. The farmers go on up to the stony end of the valley and make do, and do better than anyone expected, out of spite.

choices.text: Let the needle spin. There is room for both

mem.note: room for both

ok.log: {npc} reads the spinning needle as a sign that the valley is generous, and sites the manor on your shoulder and the farmers in the bend, with water for both. The manor's children and the farmers' children grow up throwing stones at each other, which is a kind of village.

fail.log: The spinning needle frightens the rich family off and convinces the farmers the valley is haunted. Both leave. {npc} looks at the compass for a long time and then at you, reproachfully.

events.text: {npc} is old, with a cane and a grandchild to carry the compass. {He} has sited two hundred graves in a long life, all on good ground, and never one for {his} own family. {He} climbs to the hollow under your shoulder, the best spot in the valley, and sits down there. "Here," {he} says to the ridge. "If you will have me. I will not ask it to make anyone a lord. I would just like to lie near the only dragon I ever met."

choices.text: Warm the ground under {him} through the winter, and let {him} have the spot

effects.npcPass: in the hollow under the dragon ridge, as was asked

mem.note: let me lie in its shoulder

effects.log: {npc} dies that winter and is buried in the hollow under your shoulder, with the compass. Nobody in the family becomes a lord. Nobody in the family ever has a bad harvest either, and they put that down to hard work, which is also true.

choices.text: Shift the vein a little, so the spot is good for the grandchildren too

ok.npcPass: in the hollow under the dragon ridge

mem.note: made my grave help the living

ok.log: The grandchild with the compass becomes the greatest geomancer of the age and never takes a fee from a poor family. {npc} would have liked that.

fail.npcPass: in the hollow under the dragon ridge
fail.log: You shift the vein and it slides out from under the hollow altogether. {npc} lies in plain ground, which {he} would have found very funny.

choices.text: Let a landslide close the hollow. No graves in your shoulder

mem.note: closed the hollow to me

effects.log: The rocks come down in the night. {npc} looks at them in the morning, nods, and goes home to be buried in the family's ordinary hill. {He} does not seem angry. {He} seems to have half expected it.

events.text: Across the valley from your ridge stands a ridge of pale rock, and the saddle between the two is a meadow of wild azaleas, and one spring dawn there is a tiger lying in it. Not a tiger: the Tiger. White, barred with black, larger than a house, with eyes the colour of a winter sky. It has held the right ridge of this valley since before the first house was built. It looks at you the way a landlord looks at a tenant who moved in without asking. "Left ridge," it says. "So. You are what was coming."
events.arc: The White Tiger of the Right Ridge

choices.text: Bow your head first

effects.log: You lower your head to the azaleas. The Tiger considers this for a long time and then, very slightly, lowers its own. "Manners," it says. "Good. The last one had none." It does not say what happened to the last one.

choices.text: Hold its eye until it looks away

effects.log: Neither of you looks away until the sun is up. Then the Tiger yawns, enormously, and walks off, which counts as a draw if you are generous and as a loss if you are honest.

choices.text: Ask it what it has guarded, all this time

effects.log: "The west side of the valley," says the Tiger. "Deer, boar, an old shrine, and a spring nobody has found yet. The east side was nobody's. Now it is yours. Do not make me sorry."

events.text: A great stag dies in the stream at the bottom of the valley, exactly in the middle, half on your bank and half on the Tiger's. The Tiger comes down at dusk to eat it and finds you lying there, considering it.
events.arc: The White Tiger of the Right Ridge

choices.text: Let it eat, on your side too

effects.log: The Tiger eats, watching you over the carcass. When it is done it licks its paws and says, "The stream is the line, then?" You agree that the stream is the line. It is the first treaty of the valley, and nobody human will ever know it was signed.

choices.text: Push it back to its own bank

ok.log: You shove, it shoves, and the stream comes out of its banks. In the end it backs off a pace onto its own side, not out of fear, but with an air of noting something down for later.

fail.log: It hits you once across the face. Once is enough. It eats the stag on your side, slowly, while you bleed in the stream. (-14 health)

choices.text: Propose the middle of the stream as the line, and the stag as the first shared meal

ok.log: The Tiger thinks about it. Then it tears the stag in half, neatly, and pushes your half across the water. You do not eat stag. You eat it anyway. Some treaties need a meal.

fail.log: The Tiger listens to your proposal with great patience, then eats the whole stag, then says, "Yes. Next time."

events.text: The first spring after a hard winter, the clouds come in off the sea, and they come to you: you are the dragon, the rain is yours to share. The Tiger's slope is still brown, its spring still frozen, its deer thin. It does not ask. It sits on the pale ridge and watches the clouds pile up over your side.
events.arc: The White Tiger of the Right Ridge

choices.text: Give the first rain to its slope

effects.log: The rain falls on the pale ridge first. By the end of the month the Tiger's slope is green and the deer are fat, and the Tiger comes to the saddle and lies down there without a word, which, you are learning, is how a tiger says thank you.

choices.text: Split it evenly, left and right

effects.log: Half and half. The valley floor between gets both, and that summer the people in the middle have the best harvest anyone can remember. Left ridge and right ridge, the old books say. You begin to see why.

choices.text: Keep it for your own side. You are the dragon

effects.log: Your side is green. The pale ridge stays brown until summer. The Tiger says nothing about it, at all, all year, so loudly that the whole valley feels it.

events.text: Tiger hunters. Forty of them, royal ones, with spears and bows and a banner, sent because a white tiger is the greatest prize a hunter can carry to the king, and the court pays by size. They have beaters and dogs, and they are working up the pale ridge from both ends, and by tomorrow noon they will have the Tiger between them.
events.arc: The White Tiger of the Right Ridge

choices.text: Bring a fog down over the pale ridge for three days

effects.log: For three days nobody on the pale ridge can see a spear's length. The dogs lose the scent. Two hunters fall into a gully. On the fourth day the captain declares the white tiger a legend and goes home. On the fifth day the Tiger comes to the saddle and lies down beside you, close enough to touch.

choices.text: Draw the hunters off down your own side

effects.log: You let the beaters see something long and green move in the pines of the left ridge, and forty hunters forget about the tiger at once. It takes you a month to shake them, and an arrow stays in your flank until spring. (-10 health)

choices.text: Let it fend for itself. It is a tiger

effects.log: It fends for itself. It kills three dogs and a horse and goes up the cliff where nobody can follow. Afterwards it does not come to the saddle for a long time, and when it does, it lies a little further away than before.

events.text: A long winter night on the saddle, snow on both your backs. The Tiger talks, for once. It is older than you. It has met the others: the Black Tortoise with the snake around it in the north, the Vermilion Bird over the southern sea, and once, at a distance, the Yellow Dragon of the centre, who said nothing to it at all. "They will ask me about you, one day," it says. "Tell me why you guard. So I know what to say."
events.arc: The White Tiger of the Right Ridge

choices.text: "For the people in the middle"

effects.log: The Tiger turns that over. "That is the right answer," it says. "I am not sure it is your answer yet. We will see."

choices.text: "Because I was born to it"

effects.log: "So was I," says the Tiger. "That is not a reason. That is a birth." It puts its head down on its paws and does not talk any more that night.

choices.text: "I do not know yet"

effects.log: The Tiger laughs, a sound like a rockfall a long way off. "Good," it says. "The ones who know at the start are the ones who fall." You watch the snow pile on its back until dawn, and feel, for the first time, that you are not the only one keeping this valley.

events.text: The Tiger has a cub. White, barred, the size of a dog and twice as foolish, it falls into your stream every day and has to be fished out. One spring morning the Tiger brings it to the saddle by the scruff and drops it in front of you. "I have to go west for a season," it says. "Watch it. If it dies, we are enemies. If it is spoiled, also."
events.arc: The White Tiger of the Right Ridge

choices.text: Watch it. Teach it to swim

effects.log: By the end of the season the cub can swim like an otter and has a terrible habit of riding on your head. The Tiger comes back, looks at its child sitting between your horns, and says nothing for a long time. Then: "Spoiled. But alive." It sounds pleased.

choices.text: Watch it, strictly, from a distance

effects.log: The cub survives a bear, two hunters and its own stupidity, mostly because of you, and never knows it. The Tiger, when it comes back, counts the cub's legs and nods. "Correctly done," it says. It is the most it has ever said.

choices.text: Refuse. You are not a nursemaid

effects.log: The Tiger picks the cub up by the scruff again and carries it west. It does not ask you for anything else for a hundred years.

events.text: A family comes up the valley with everything they own on two A-frames: a cooking pot, a hoe, a sack of seed millet, a hen, and four children. Burnt-field farmers from the high hills, whose fields have given out. {npc}, who leads them, walks the valley floor for a whole day, and stops where the stream bends under your elbow, and puts down the A-frame. "Here," {he} says. "The water winds. The ridge holds it. Here."

choices.text: Breathe spring over their first field

mem.note: made the first field come up green

effects.log: The millet comes up in nine days instead of twenty. The children run along the rows shouting. {npc} kneels in the dirt, takes up a handful, and looks up at the ridge for a long, long time.

choices.text: Move a boulder in the night so they build a little higher up the bank

mem.note: moved the boulder for me

ok.log: In the morning there is a boulder where the house was going to go. {npc} curses it, then builds above it. The next summer the stream floods to exactly the boulder's edge and no further. {npc} goes out and pats the boulder, and does not say anything to anyone.

fail.log: The boulder rolls into the stream and makes a ford. {npc} is delighted with the ford and builds exactly where {he} meant to. The flood, when it comes, takes the hen house. Next time, perhaps, a smaller boulder.

choices.text: Watch them, and do nothing yet

effects.log: Mud, straw, river stones, a thatch of reeds. By the first frost there is a house with smoke coming out of it, under your elbow. You did not do anything. You find you are very proud of them anyway.

events.text: {npc} has built an altar at the foot of the ridge: three flat stones, one on two, nothing fancy. Every dawn, before anything else, {he} draws the first water from the stream and sets it on the stone in a white bowl, bows twice, and goes to work. Not for the mountain spirit. Not for the ancestors. For the ridge. {He} could not tell you why. You know exactly why: someone did that for you once, at a well, on a first full moon.

choices.text: Drink the first water every morning, so the bowl is empty when {he} comes back

mem.note: took every offering from my bowl

effects.log: The bowl is always empty by the time {npc} comes back from the field. {He} tells nobody, and fills it again the next morning, and the next, for years.

choices.text: Leave the water, and put a river pebble in the bowl, green as your scales

mem.note: left a green stone in my bowl

effects.log: {npc} finds the pebble and keeps it in the family's rice jar, where it stays for nine generations. Their rice jar is never empty, which is mostly because they are hard workers, and partly not.

choices.text: Let the water stand. Gifts are not for taking

effects.log: The water stands in the bowl all day, reflecting the ridge. {npc} pours it back into the stream at dusk. It becomes a family rule: the first water to the ridge, the last water back to the stream.

events.text: There are five houses at the bend now, and they have dug a well together: stone-lined, with a wooden lid and a rope worn smooth. {npc} is old and lame, and on the first full moon of the year {he} has the grandchildren carry {him} to the well at first cockcrow, to draw the first water, the way it was done in the old village. The first water of the year, they say, carries the dragon's luck.

choices.text: Lay one scale on the stones at the bottom of the well

mem.note: shone a green light in the first water

effects.log: The bucket comes up with a green light in it that fades as it reaches the air. {npc} sees it. Everybody else sees water. {npc} drinks the first cup and laughs like a child, and tells the grandchildren the dragon is in the well, and they believe it for the rest of their lives.

choices.text: Make the first water sweet, and nothing more

effects.log: It is the sweetest water anyone in the valley has ever tasted. The well becomes famous. People walk a day to draw from it on the first full moon, which brings trade, which brings more houses.

choices.text: Stay away from the well. It is theirs now

effects.log: The water is ordinary water. {npc} drinks it and is content. It is, you think, a good thing for a village to have a well that is only a well.

events.text: The bend has twelve houses, a threshing floor, a shrine, a carved pair of village guardians at the entrance with bulging eyes and painted grins, and a tall pole with a wooden duck on top, looking south. It has a name, too. They call it Yonggok: Dragon's Elbow. Nobody remembers who started calling it that. You do. It was the grandchildren.

choices.text: Wake the green over the whole valley floor that spring

effects.log: Twelve houses, and every field green a month early. A thirteenth house goes up in autumn, and a fourteenth. Somewhere in the Eastern Palace a room is filling up.

choices.text: Hold back. A village that gets everything learns nothing

effects.log: An ordinary year: some fields good, some bad, everyone grumbling. The village learns to share seed, dig ditches, mend each other's roofs. They will need that, later, when you are busy.

choices.text: Let the duck on the pole see you, once, at dusk

effects.log: Somebody else sees you too: a girl bringing in the goats. By morning the whole of Dragon's Elbow knows why it is called that, and the name stops being a joke.

events.text: A funeral comes up your flank: mourners in coarse hemp, the bier heaped with paper flowers, a bell, a geomancer in front with a compass. They dig where the geomancer points, and the geomancer has pointed well: the spot is a hand's width above the place where your vein runs closest to the skin. Bury a father here, the books say, and the sons will be lords. The eldest son weeps for show. The youngest weeps for real.

choices.text: Let your qi flow into the grave

effects.log: You let it run, warm, into the old man in the ground. You feel his bones take it, the way dry earth takes rain. Somewhere in a market town, three sons wake up luckier than they went to sleep.

choices.text: Shift your vein a hand's width, so the grave sits on nothing

effects.log: They bury him on good dry ordinary ground. The family prospers exactly as much as it works. The geomancer, years later, comes back with the compass and frowns at it, and taps it, and frowns.

choices.text: Let it work, but only for the son who wept for real

ok.log: It is a fine piece of work, steering luck down one branch of a family and not the others. The youngest son's barley never fails. The eldest son's schemes do, every one, and he never understands why.

fail.log: Luck is not that easy to aim. It goes to all three sons, in equal measure, and you suspect the eldest will make the worst use of it.

events.text: The sons have risen. The youngest has a farm of a hundred fields and gives half the harvest away in bad years. The eldest has bought a post as a county magistrate and is the cruellest official in the province: grain seized, men flogged for the levy, a daughter taken for a debt. Every spring he comes in a sedan chair to bow at his father's grave in your flank, and thank it.

choices.text: Pull your vein back from the grave

effects.log: The luck drains out of the grave like water from a cracked jar. Within three years the eldest son is impeached; within five he is in exile. The youngest loses some fields too, and does not complain. Luck is a blunt tool.

choices.text: Keep it flowing. The valley gets the youngest son's grain

effects.log: The magistrate grows rich and cruel and old. The youngest son feeds three villages through a famine. You tell yourself it balances. It does not, quite, and you know it.

choices.text: Let the magistrate's sedan chair slide off the path, gently, every spring

effects.log: Every spring, at the same bend, the bearers slip and the magistrate lands in the mud before his father's grave. By the fifth year the whole province is laughing about it. A laughed-at magistrate is, it turns out, a much less frightening one.

events.text: A stolen grave. In the dead of night a second family comes up your flank with spades and a small bundle of bones, and buries their own grandfather just above the first grave, to steal its luck. They do it quickly, cover it with turf, and creep away. By spring the first family will find it, and then there will be a lawsuit that lasts three generations.

choices.text: Bring a little landslide down and push the stolen bones out onto the path

effects.log: The first family finds a bundle of bones on the path in the morning and is horrified, and the second family has to come and collect their grandfather in daylight in front of everyone. Nobody steals a grave on your ridge again for two hundred years.

choices.text: Let both old men lie there and share

effects.log: There is enough vein for two grandfathers. The two families go to law anyway, for years, and in the end their grandchildren meet at the court, and that, eventually, is a wedding. Graves do strange things.

choices.text: Let the stolen grave sit on dry ground and the true one keep the vein

ok.log: The thieves wait twenty years for their luck to turn and it never does. In the end they move the bones themselves, at night, ashamed, and nobody ever knows.

fail.log: You split the vein between them by accident and neither grave gets enough. Both families decline, a little, and blame each other, a lot.

events.text: Forty years on, the clan of the first grave holds its ancestral rite at your flank every autumn: two hundred people in white, a table of food, a great-grandson reading the old man's name off a tablet. Their genealogy book says the family's fortune comes from a dragon vein in the ridge, discovered by a wise ancestor. It does not mention you. It mentions the geomancer.

choices.text: Let them believe it was the geomancer

effects.log: The geomancer's descendants become very famous on the strength of it. You find, to your surprise, that you do not mind at all.

choices.text: Stir the pines on the ridge during the rite, so they know whose ridge it is

effects.log: Two hundred people in white look up as the whole ridge sighs in a windless noon. The great-grandson drops the tablet. A new line goes into the genealogy book, in very large characters.

choices.text: Ask nothing. Send the clan's poorest branch a better harvest

effects.log: The poorest branch of the clan, who stand at the back of the rite and are not given the good food, have a remarkable year. They do not know why. They give some of it to the rite, the next autumn, and are moved up a row.

events.text: Hammering in the night. Four men with lanterns and sledgehammers, and a fifth with a compass and a chart, on the narrow saddle of your neck where the vein runs shallow. They are driving iron: stakes as long as a spear, black, square-sided, into the rock. Iron. Every blow goes through you like a hot needle, and below in the valley, though nobody there knows it yet, the wells begin very slowly to go down.

choices.text: Shake the ridge and throw them off

ok.log: The ridge heaves. Lanterns go flying, men go flying, and the five of them run downhill in the dark leaving one stake in the rock and the rest in the bracken. One is enough to hurt. You lie there with it in your neck until dawn.

fail.log: The iron has already got into you. You cannot shake properly; you shudder, and they hold on and finish the job. Two stakes, deep in your neck. Below, a spring stops. (-8 health)

choices.text: Lie still and count the blows, so you know their pattern

effects.log: Three stakes, four blows each, at points the chart picked very carefully. They know what they are doing. That is the worst of it. In the morning, the valley's wells are a hand lower and nobody knows why.

choices.text: Pull the first stake out with your teeth while they are still hammering the second

effects.log: The hammerer looks up to see the stake he has just driven come back out of the rock, held in a mouth the size of a doorway. Nobody stays for the third. Your mouth is burnt for a month. (-15 health)

events.text: The one with the compass goes down to the inn at the ford afterwards and drinks alone. {npc}: a geomancer who failed the examinations twice, a scholar's hat gone shiny at the brim, a purse that is fuller tonight than it has been in years. {He} keeps looking at the ridge through the inn door. {He} knows what {he} has done. {He} did it anyway.

choices.text: Follow {him} home, to see who pays

effects.log: Three days of travel to a market town, and a tiled gate, and a steward who counts out silver for {npc} without looking at {him}. The house belongs to a landlord who has been buying up the valley's debts. A valley whose wells fail is a valley whose farmers sell cheap.

choices.text: Show yourself in the inn doorway

mem.note: watched me through the inn door

ok.log: {npc} sees a green eye in the doorway, as big as the door. {He} goes very white, gets up, walks out past you up the ridge in the dark, and pulls one of the stakes out with bleeding hands. Then {he} runs, and keeps running for years.

mem.note: watched me through the inn door

fail.log: {npc} sees the eye and screams and does not repent at all. {He} learns something much worse: that the ridge is alive, and therefore can be killed.

choices.text: Leave {him} to the drink

effects.log: {npc} finishes the jar, and another, and sleeps on the bench, and in the morning leaves by the south road. You will see that face again. You do not know that yet.

events.text: The landlord in the market town has a ledger. In it are the debts of every farmer in your valley, bought cheap from the moneylenders, and next to each name a number: the price the land will fetch when the wells fail and the harvests fail and the farmers sell. He has never seen a dragon. He does not believe in them. He believes in geomancers, and pays them by the stake.

choices.text: Bring a landslide down on his granary

effects.log: The granary goes in a night, under half a hillside. The landlord comes to look at it in the morning, and stands there a long time, and then, being a practical man, sells the valley debts back to the farmers at a loss and moves his business to the coast.

choices.text: Make the valley prosper anyway, louder than iron

effects.log: You pour yourself into the fields until the stakes in your neck scream. The harvest is the best in a decade. The farmers pay their debts. The landlord looks at his ledger for a long time and crosses the valley out. (-6 health)

choices.text: Visit him in a dream of iron, and let him feel every stake

ok.log: You cannot yet send a true dream, but you can lean on a sleeping mind the way the iron leans on you. He wakes screaming nine nights in a row. On the tenth he sends men to pull the stakes, and never says why.

fail.log: You lean on his sleep and he does not even dream. Some people are made of ledger all the way through. (-5 health)

events.text: The stakes are still in you: black iron in the saddle of your neck, rusting slowly, and the rust goes into the vein like poison into a well. The valley has had two thin harvests. A dragon can pull iron out of itself. A dragon also knows exactly how much it will hurt.

choices.text: Pull them all in one night

effects.log: One by one, with your teeth, while the moon crosses the sky. Your mouth is iron and fire. By dawn there are only holes in the rock, and the springs in the valley run again before noon. (-20 health)

choices.text: One a year, as you can bear it

effects.log: One stake, one spring. The valley recovers slowly and never knows what from. You come to know the taste of iron like an old enemy's name. (-6 health)

choices.text: Ask the White Tiger to help

effects.log: The Tiger comes over the saddle and pulls with you, its jaws on the iron beside yours. Iron does not burn a tiger. When it is done it spits rust and says, "You owe me a deer." You owe it a great deal more than a deer. (-8 health)

events.text: {npc} is back, and is not alone. Older, harder, a scholar's robe traded for a dark coat with deep pockets, and behind {him} five apprentices with hammers, each carrying a bundle of black iron. {He} has made a trade of it, a school of it: the vein-cutters. Somewhere in the market towns, people have started paying {him} to kill the luck of their enemies' valleys. And {he} has come back to the first ridge {he} ever pierced, to finish it.

choices.text: Bring the whole saddle of the ridge down on them

ok.log: The ridge shrugs. Half the saddle goes down the north face in a roar of rock and pine, and the iron with it. {npc} is pulled out of the rubble by the apprentices, alive, with both legs broken, and carried off swearing an oath you can hear from the head of the valley.

fail.log: {npc} has been waiting years for you to move. The first stake goes in exactly where your heart vein is closest to the rock.
fail.deathCause: an iron stake through the heart vein, driven by the vein-cutters' founder

choices.text: Fog the ridge so thick they cannot find the vein

effects.log: They hammer blind for three nights and put most of the iron into plain rock. One stake finds you. {npc} feels it go home, and smiles, and leaves knowing that next time {he} will need a better chart.

choices.text: Let {npc} see the valley first: the houses, the well, the children

mem.note: showed me the children of the valley

ok.log: You bend the fog so that it opens on the village at dusk: smoke, lamps, a child carrying water. {npc} stands looking at it for a long time. Then {he} sends the apprentices home and goes away alone. The vein-cutters go on without {him}. But not here, not for a while.

fail.log: {npc} looks at the valley and says, "Yes. That is what the client wants gone." Two stakes before dawn.

events.text: A vein-cutter's scout on your ridge again: a young apprentice with a chart and a bag of iron pegs, pacing your neck, counting steps, marking places with chalk. The school of iron has not forgotten you. It sends someone every few years, the way a moneylender sends a boy to knock.

choices.text: Scare the scout off the ridge

effects.log: The chalk marks are gone in the morning and so is the scout, and the chart is in the stream. The school will send another. You will scare that one too.

choices.text: Let the scout map a false vein, far from your heart
