ok.log: You shift the warmth in the rock so the chart shows a vein along the empty north slope. Some years later a team of cutters drives forty stakes into nothing at all and goes home very pleased.

fail.log: The scout is better than the chart looks. One peg goes in true before you notice.

choices.text: Pull the scout's pegs out every night and leave them in a neat pile

effects.log: Every morning, a neat pile of pegs at the scout's feet. On the fifth morning the scout sits down beside the pile and laughs, and goes home to say the ridge is not worth the iron. (-4 health)

events.text: Winter, and smoke over the mountains to the north. A sect war, the kind that comes every generation: the Black Pine Gate has been broken by its neighbours and its village burned. Now its people are coming over the snow of your saddle, two hundred of them, old people and children and wounded disciples in torn grey. And your village knows that grey. Forty years ago, the Black Pine Gate's disciples took the village's whole harvest at sword point. The village is at the foot of the pass with torches and hoes. Above you the fourth mansion, the Room, waits: the star of taking in.

choices.text: Open the pass with a warm wind

effects.log: A warm wind out of nowhere melts the drifts on the saddle in an hour. The refugees come down the path in the dusk, slowly, toward the torches. Nobody on either side knows what to do. That is a beginning.

choices.text: Close the pass with snow

effects.log: You breathe out and the saddle fills with snow to the height of a house. The refugees stop, and stand, and turn east along the ridge toward the next pass, which is three days further. The village goes home relieved. You lie under the snow and feel the Room star like a cold hand.

choices.text: Do nothing. Let them meet and choose

effects.log: You let it happen. The refugees come down. The torches stay lit across the path all night. Nobody moves. At dawn a refugee child walks up to the line and asks a village child for water, and the village child, not knowing any better, gives it.

events.text: The village will not let the refugees into the houses. So they camp in the snow in the hollow of your elbow, two hundred people around a few fires of green wood, and on the third night the cold comes down from the north like an iron lid. By morning the old ones and the small ones will be dead. Your elbow is the only shelter in the valley. It is also part of you.

choices.text: Curl the ridge around them, and keep them warm with your own body

effects.log: The ridge closes a little, like an arm. The ground in the hollow is warm all night, warm as a heated floor, and the snow melts off the tents. Two hundred people sleep in the crook of your elbow, and nobody dies. You are cold for a year after. (-12 health)

choices.text: Send the village headman a sign: a warm spring breaking out at the gate

ok.log: A hot spring breaks out of the frozen ground at the village gate in the night, steaming. The headman, an old person who still remembers the bad year, stands looking at it until sunrise, and then opens the threshing barn to the refugees.

fail.log: The spring comes up in the wrong place, out in the paddies, and the headman takes it for a bad omen. In the end you warm the hollow yourself. (-10 health)

choices.text: It is their quarrel. Leave it to the morning

effects.log: In the morning there are eleven small bundles in the snow. The village buries them, out of shame, and lets the rest into the barns. The Room star does not light. A room that opened too late is still a door that was shut.

events.text: In the thaw, the woodcutters find the refugees' trail along the ridge to the eastern pass. It is easy to follow. There are things left beside it: a pot, a shoe, a cradle-board, a grave scraped in the snow. A last group of stragglers, thirty or so, is still on the ridge, on your back, too weak to go on.

choices.text: Carry them down into the valley on your back, at night

effects.log: Thirty people wake in the morning in the threshing barn of the village with no memory of the night except that the mountain moved. The village, who did not invite them and does not know how they got there, gives them gruel, because what else can you do. (-10 health)

choices.text: Keep the pass shut. You chose

effects.log: The stragglers move on east along the ridge, very slowly, and you do not watch to see how many reach the pass. The Room star stays dark over the valley.

events.text: The victors come. Thirty disciples of the sect that broke the Black Pine Gate, in red and black, with a list of names: the survivors who escaped, the ones still worth killing. They ride into the village at noon, and the headman stands in the road, and behind the headman the refugees who live in the barns now go very quiet. The village could hand them over and be safe. The village is looking at the ridge.

choices.text: Stand up out of the ridge behind the headman

effects.log: The ridge rises. Pines slide off your back. Your head comes up over the village roofs with the noon sun behind it and looks down at thirty riders. Nobody needs to say anything. They turn and ride north and do not come back. In the Eastern Palace the Room star lights: the house that takes in the stranger. It is a grand way to light it. You enjoyed it a little too much.

choices.text: Fog the valley and fold the refugees into the hollow of your elbow, out of sight

ok.log: For three days the riders search the valley in a fog so thick they lose each other. Every barn they open is empty. In the hollow of your elbow, a hundred and eighty people sit very still in the warm dark, children asleep, nobody breathing loudly. On the fourth day the riders leave. The Room star lights over the valley like a lamp in a window.

fail.log: The fog thins on the second day and the riders find the hollow. You come up out of the ridge to drive them off, and they go, but with two of the refugee fighters dead and your flank cut open by a blade that knew what dragons are. (-14 health)

choices.text: Let the village give up the refugee fighters, and keep the rest

effects.log: Six people in grey walk out to the riders of their own accord, so the village will not have to choose. They are taken north. The village keeps the others and is ashamed, and kind to them forever after, out of the shame. The Room star does not light.

events.text: Twenty years on, at the threshing floor of the village, a wedding: a village grandchild and a refugee grandchild, in the red and blue, with a wild goose of carved wood on the table between them. Half the guests have grandparents who held torches at the pass. The other half have grandparents who came down it. They are all very merry on the same rice liquor and arguing about whose grandparents were braver.

choices.text: Send a warm wind and blossom over the threshing floor

effects.log: Plum blossom in a cold month, falling on the bride and the groom and the argument. Both sides take it as proof their grandparents were right. That is, you think, as close as a valley ever gets to peace.

choices.text: Let the wedding be theirs

effects.log: You lie still and listen to the drums. The valley that would not let strangers in has made strangers into cousins without any help from you. A room, it turns out, is something the people inside build.

events.text: You find you can do a new thing. On a spring night you lean the whole weight of the ridge, very gently, against the sleep of the valley, and you are inside it: a hundred dreams, like a hundred lamps behind paper windows. In three of the houses in the village, a child is coming. In this country everybody knows what it means to dream of a dragon before a birth. You choose a lamp, and go in, blue-green and enormous, and coil down into a sleeper's lap. Nine months later the child is born, and the midwife says {npc} cried like thunder.

choices.text: The house of the potter, the poorest in the village

mem.note: came down into the dream before I was born

effects.log: The potter's household is so poor the dream is the only thing of value in it, and they keep it like gold: secret, as the old women say a good dream must be kept. {npc} grows up in a house that smells of wet clay, and does not know why the ridge seems to watch over the yard.

choices.text: The headman's house, where a child could do the most good

mem.note: came down into the dream before I was born

effects.log: The headman's household cannot keep a secret. By noon the whole valley knows the child will be great, and by the time {npc} can walk, {npc} has heard it a thousand times. That is a heavy thing to carry on small shoulders.

choices.text: The refugee family in the old barn, who came over the pass

mem.note: came down into the dream before I was born

effects.log: A dragon dream in the refugees' barn. Half the village is outraged and half is moved, and an aunt from the headman's house offers a bolt of silk to buy the dream, as people do. The refugee family will not sell. {npc} is born in the barn, under the ridge, and nobody can ever again say the refugees are not of the valley.

events.text: {npc} is seven, and has found the warm rock on the ridge, the one at the base of your left horn, and comes up every evening to sit on it and talk. Nobody told {him} to. {He} talks to the ridge exactly as {he} would to a big, slow friend who cannot answer yet: about the potter's kiln, about the other children, about a dream {he} keeps having, of something green and very long that comes down out of the stars.

choices.text: Warm the rock

mem.note: kept the rock warm for me

effects.log: The rock is always warm. {npc} falls asleep on it most evenings and has to be fetched down by lantern. The family stops worrying about it. Everyone knows the ridge is safe.

choices.text: Let a single pine cone roll down to {his} feet whenever {he} asks a question

mem.note: pine cones for answers

effects.log: {npc} works out the system within a month: one cone for yes, none for no. The questions get bigger every year. You answer them all honestly, which is harder than it sounds with pine cones.

choices.text: Stay quiet. The child must have a life that is not about you

effects.log: {npc} keeps coming for a year and then, slowly, comes less, and plays with the other children more. It is the right thing. You miss the evenings anyway.

events.text: {npc} is thirteen when the scout comes: a sword-bearing disciple from a sect beyond the mountains, testing children's roots in the villages, taking the gifted ones away for training. {npc}'s meridians, the scout says, are like nothing the scout has ever seen: green, somehow, and very wide. The scout wants {him} now, tonight. The family is frightened, and proud, and does not know what to say.

choices.text: Let {him} go, and send the wind after the scout, warning

mem.note: let me go to the sect

effects.log: The scout's hat blows off at the valley mouth, and blows off again at the pass, and again at the river, nine times in a day. The scout gets the message and treats {npc} very carefully indeed.

choices.text: Close the pass in the night. {He} is too young

mem.note: kept me in the valley

effects.log: A rockfall closes the pass for a season. The scout leaves by the long road, alone, muttering about cursed valleys. {npc} stays, and grows up at home, and spends years wondering what might have been.

choices.text: Let {him} choose: hold the wind still and wait

mem.note: let me choose

effects.log: {npc} climbs to the warm rock in the night and sits there till dawn, deciding. You do not move a needle. In the morning {npc} goes down and tells the scout: in five years, when I am grown. The scout, surprised, agrees.

events.text: {npc} is grown, with a bundle on one shoulder and a borrowed sword on the other, at the valley mouth where the stream winds out. {He} is going out into the murim, the wide world of sects and swords and debts of blood. {He} turns at the bend and looks back at the ridge for a long time, the way {he} looked at it as a child, and says aloud: "If you are what I think you are, give me something to remember you by."

choices.text: Rise, once, all of you, for {him} alone

mem.note: rose out of the ridge when I left

effects.log: The ridge stands up out of the morning mist, green and gold and nine li long, and looks down at one young person at the bend of a stream. {npc} does not bow. {He} laughs, and shouts something the wind takes away, and goes out into the world as someone who has seen a dragon. That is not always a gift.

choices.text: Give {him} nothing but a hard wind in the face. The world will be harder

mem.note: met me with a cold wind at the valley mouth

effects.log: A cold wind straight down the valley, hard enough to make {npc} lean into it. {He} stands there a long while, then turns and walks into it, head down, which is, you think, what the world will ask. Whether {he} understood or only felt refused, you will find out.

choices.text: Let a green scale fall at {his} feet, and let {him} go free of you

mem.note: dropped a green scale at my feet at the bend of the stream

effects.log: A single scale, green as new leaves and as big as a palm, drops onto the path. {npc} picks it up, and wraps it in a cloth, and puts it inside {his} robe, over the heart. Then {he} goes. What becomes of {him} out there is {his} own, now. That is what a dream is for.

events.text: A sect scout on the ridge: {npc}, a senior disciple of the Clear Spring Sect in a white robe, with a sword, a surveyor's rope and a pot of ink. {He} is mapping your valley for a mountain gate. A sect needs a mountain with good qi for its cultivation halls, water for its kitchens, and a village below to feed it, and your valley, {npc} writes in a neat hand, has all three, and something else besides that {he} cannot quite name.

choices.text: Let {him} feel the qi of the ridge, and welcome {him}

effects.log: {npc} sits down to meditate on your shoulder and gets up three days later with eyes like lamps. The report to the sect elders runs to forty pages. Most of them are about the ridge.

choices.text: Lose {his} rope in the fog, three times

effects.log: Three ropes, three fogs. {npc} gives up surveying, sits down in the bracken, and says to the ridge, "You do not want us. I understand. I shall tell them." You suspect {he} will tell them something else entirely.

choices.text: Shake a landslide down across the survey line

ok.log: Half a slope across the survey line. {npc} looks at it, then at the ridge, and writes in the report that the valley is unstable. You have bought perhaps a generation.

fail.log: The slope slides the wrong way and nearly buries a woodcutter. {npc} pulls the woodcutter out, and writes in the report that the valley needs protecting. (-6 health)

events.text: The Clear Spring Sect comes in person: an elder in white with a jade fan, twelve disciples, a cart of gifts for the village. The bargain is simple. A mountain gate on your shoulder, halls on your back, a sect's protection for the village against bandits and worse. In return, the upper fields, the sacred grove, and the village's sons and daughters as servants and disciples. The headman does not know how to say no to a sword. The headman looks at the ridge.

choices.text: Bloom the azaleas over the elder's tent, all at once

effects.log: Azaleas, in autumn, all over the elder's tent. The elder takes it, correctly, as consent, and bows to the ridge with real respect. The sect builds carefully, asks before it cuts, and keeps the bargain better than most.

choices.text: Let the village decide, without signs

effects.log: The village argues for a month and then, being a village, splits the difference: the gate, but not the grove. The elder is annoyed and accepts. Human compromises are untidy and last surprisingly well.

choices.text: Drop a great pine across the path to the gate site, every morning

effects.log: Nine mornings, nine pines. On the tenth the elder sits down on the latest one and says to the ridge, quite calmly, "I see. Then we will be your neighbours, not your tenants." The sect builds its gate on the far side of the river, and visits.

events.text: A second sect, and this one does not ask. The Blood Lotus Cult comes over the north pass at night with crimson banners and a cart of iron chains: a demonic sect that has heard there is a living dragon vein in this valley. Their arts drink qi from the land the way a leech drinks from a leg, and a dragon's qi is the richest there is. Before dawn they have chained your neck with a circle of blood-written talismans, and begun to drink.

choices.text: Rise and break the chains

ok.log: You stand up out of the ridge with the chains on you and they snap like straw rope. Lanterns go flying. The cult leader, a pale person with very red lips, looks up at you and smiles, and goes back over the pass with the survivors to think about it.

fail.log: The talismans hold. They drink.
fail.deathCause: drained by the Blood Lotus Cult through a ring of blood talismans

choices.text: Sink deep into the ridge, out of their reach, and wait for help

effects.log: You go down into the rock, far below the chains, and they drink only what is near the surface: the springs, the pines, a year of the valley's luck. At dawn the Clear Spring Sect comes over the river with swords. (-14 health)

choices.text: Pour so much qi into the chains that the talismans burn

ok.log: They wanted to drink. You give them a river. The talismans catch fire one by one, and the cultists holding the chains are thrown across the valley. It is the first time you understand that a dragon can win by giving.

fail.log: They drink faster than you can give. You lie half-empty under the chains until the righteous sect drives them off. (-16 health)

events.text: The battle comes down into the valley. White robes from the river, crimson from the pass, and the village in the middle, where the paddies are. Swords flash over the threshing floor. A cultist sets the shrine on fire. A righteous disciple uses a farmer's cart as a shield, with the farmer still in it.

choices.text: Curl around the village and let the sects fight outside

effects.log: You put the ridge around the village like an arm round a child. Swords bounce off your scales all afternoon. Not one villager dies. The sects fight in the river and the paddies until dark, and neither of them ever forgets the arm. (-10 health)

choices.text: Strike the Blood Lotus. Only them

effects.log: Your tail comes down on the crimson banners like the side of a mountain. The cult breaks and runs north. The Clear Spring Sect cheers, and the elder bows, and writes to the capital that the dragon of the valley has joined the righteous path. You have not joined anything. They write it anyway.

choices.text: Strike both. The valley is not a battlefield

ok.log: White and crimson alike go into the river. Both sects leave the valley that night. Neither will come back for a hundred years. The village is safe, and terrified, and very careful with its offerings.

fail.log: Two sects at once is too many. They both turn on you, and the valley watches its dragon bleed. In the end they both leave, but not because of you. (-20 health)

events.text: Fifteen years on. {npc}, the scout who first mapped your valley, is an elder now, with grey in a long topknot and a jade fan of {his} own. {He} comes up to the warm rock on your shoulder without any disciples, sits down, and says to the ridge: "The sect wants to build you a shrine. A big one, with your image in gold. I have come to ask whether you want that, because nobody else in the sect will think to ask."

choices.text: Let a pine cone fall: yes

mem.note: wanted the golden shrine

effects.log: The shrine is magnificent. Pilgrims come from three provinces. Incense rises from your shoulder every day. It is very pleasant. That is exactly the danger, and you know it, and you go on enjoying it.

choices.text: Let no cone fall: no

mem.note: did not want gold

effects.log: {npc} nods, as if {he} expected it, and goes back down and argues the sect out of it for three years. In the end they build a small stone altar instead, with a bowl for water. {npc} fills it every morning, personally, until {he} is too old to climb.

choices.text: Roll a cone and then a second cone: something smaller

mem.note: settled for something smaller with me

effects.log: {npc} laughs out loud. "Something smaller. I will tell them." The shrine is a wooden pavilion with a carved green dragon on the beam, done by a village carpenter who has seen you once, and got it more or less right.

events.text: The east end of your ridge runs down to the sea as a line of cliffs, and on the cliffs the azaleas are out. Along the coast road below comes the new governor's household, and in a palanquin, the governor's lady: the most beautiful person on the east coast, people say, and they say it a great deal. She sees the azaleas on the cliff and wants one. Nobody in the escort will climb. Then an old man herding a single cow puts down the rope, climbs the cliff like a boy, picks a branch, and brings it down to her with a little song he makes up on the spot.

choices.text: Hold the cliff steady under the old man's feet

effects.log: He climbs a cliff no one could climb, because the rock under his hands does not crumble once. The lady takes the flowers and laughs. The song he sang is still sung on that coast. Nobody knows you were in it.

choices.text: Watch her from the waves

effects.log: You lie in the green water under the cliff and watch the lady with the azaleas, and something in you that has been a ridge for a long time remembers being a dragon of the deep. You do not like the feeling. You do not stop watching.

choices.text: Blow the branch down to her feet before the old man can reach it

effects.log: A gust off the sea snaps an azalea branch and lays it at her feet. The old man, halfway up, looks round, cheated. She does not pick the branch up. She waits for the old man. You find that you are, absurdly, jealous of a cowherd.

events.text: Two days down the coast road, the governor's household stops at a pavilion by the sea for the noon meal. The lady sits alone on the rocks at the water's edge, looking out. Under the sea, at the foot of your cliffs, there are caves full of green light, and further down, the old stories say, the Dragon King's palace. You could take her there. It would be very easy. She is looking straight at the place where you are.

choices.text: Take her into the deep

effects.log: The sea stands up and folds over the rocks, and when it goes down she is gone. The escort shouts. The governor falls on the shore. You carry her down through the green into the caves, and she is not afraid, which you had not expected. She asks the names of the fish.

choices.text: Rise and let her see you, only her

effects.log: Your head comes up out of the sea in front of her, close enough to touch, and goes down again. She does not scream. She smiles, as if she had been waiting all her life to be looked at by something that wanted nothing. The escort sees nothing. She never tells them.

choices.text: Go back up the coast to your valley

effects.log: You turn and go, back up the cliffs and along the ridge, and lie down in the valley with the sea-light still in your eyes. A ridge has no business with the deep. You remind yourself of that for a whole spring.

events.text: On the third day the whole coast comes to the shore. Fishermen, salt-boilers, farmers, the governor's escort, hundreds of them, each with a stick. An old man told them what to do: the mouths of many can melt iron. So they strike the rocks with their sticks, all together, and sing a song made up for the day: turtle, turtle, give her back, the sin of taking another's wife is great, if you will not give her back we will catch you in a net and roast you. The rocks ring. The song comes down through the water into the green caves, and the lady, listening, laughs.

choices.text: Give her back at once, with gifts from the deep

effects.log: You carry her up and set her on the rocks among the sticks, with pearls in her hair and the smell of the Dragon King's palace on her clothes, a smell no one on that coast has ever smelt. The crowd stops singing. The governor weeps. For the rest of her life, the lady is asked what the deep was like, and she only ever answers: very polite.

choices.text: Hold out one more day

ok.log: One more day of song, and you give her back at dusk. The song is so good by then that it goes into the books. The lady says the extra day was the best of the three.

fail.log: On the fourth day the song changes to nets, and three boats come out with iron hooks, and the shame of it goes through you like iron. You give her back torn and furious, and the coast does not forgive you for a generation. (-10 health)

choices.text: Give her back, and stay ashamed under the cliff for a year

effects.log: You set her on the shore, unharmed, and slide back into the sea before the singing has stopped. You lie under the cliffs for a whole year with the song in your ears. A crowd of farmers with sticks has taught you more about humility than forty years of lying still.

events.text: Years later. On the coast road under your cliffs there is a little stone pavilion now, and every spring when the azaleas come out, women from the fishing villages climb to the cliff top and leave branches on the rocks below, for the sea. Nobody remembers the governor's name. Everybody remembers hers, and the old man's song, and the green shape the fishermen swear they saw.

choices.text: Rise among the azalea branches in the spring tide

effects.log: The tide comes in pink with flowers, and in the middle of it a long green back, once. A fisherman sees it and the coast talks about nothing else for a year.

choices.text: Send the fishing boats good weather every azalea season

effects.log: Every spring, while the azaleas are out, the sea is gentle. The fishermen notice in the second year. By the tenth, the azalea season is the season boats are launched and children are named.

choices.text: Stay away from the cliffs. Let it be her story, not yours

effects.log: You keep to the valley. The story keeps to the coast. Somewhere between the two, you think, is where a dragon ought to live.

events.text: Royal surveyors in the valley: officials with ropes and stakes, a court geomancer with a silver-inlaid compass, and a cart with a yellow banner. The king has chosen a new site for a palace, flat land at the foot of your ridge, with your shoulder for its back and the stream for its moat. The stakes go in along your flank: wooden, thank heaven. By autumn the foundation stones are coming up the river on barges, each the size of a house.

choices.text: Let them build. A palace is a kind of shelter

effects.log: Granite blocks, a thousand labourers, a road. The valley has never been so busy, or so tired. The corvee takes the young men from every village for a season. That is what a palace costs.

choices.text: Show yourself to the surveyors, once, at dusk

effects.log: The court geomancer sees a long green shape in the mist on the ridge and drops the compass. The report goes to the capital. The court decides it is an excellent omen and builds faster.

choices.text: Wait for the king

effects.log: You lie still and let the stones come. Whatever you do about this palace, you want the king to see it with his own eyes.

events.text: The king comes to see the foundations: young, in a gold crown with jade pendants that shiver as he walks, a crowd of courtiers, and a parasol. The great blocks are in. The halls will go up in spring. He stands in the middle of the foundation where his throne will be and looks up at your ridge, and says to the court geomancer, "It feels as if the mountain is watching."

choices.text: Rise out of the foundations in full sight of the king

effects.log: The earth opens between the great blocks and you come up out of it, green and gold in the morning, higher than any hall will ever be. The courtiers lie flat. The king does not. He looks at you for a long time. Then he says, very quietly, "Not a palace, then." The chroniclers write that a yellow dragon appeared, because yellow is the colour of kings. You are green. You let it go.

choices.text: Rise at night, only for the master builder

ok.log: The old master builder sees you by lantern light and goes to the king at dawn and says, in the plain speech of builders, that this ground belongs to something else, and a palace on it will never stand easy. The king, who trusts builders more than geomancers, listens.

fail.log: The master builder sees you and decides it was the rice liquor. The palace goes up.

choices.text: Stay down. Let the palace be a palace

effects.log: The halls go up in spring, red pillars and blue-green tiles, the colour of your scales, by coincidence. The king lives under your shoulder. So does the court, and the court's appetites.

events.text: The palace is a temple now. Monks in grey where the courtiers were to be, a bronze bell where the throne was to be, and the great foundation blocks carrying a golden hall instead of a royal one. They have named it for the dragon that appeared. Every dawn the bell is struck, and every dawn you feel it in your ribs, a long low note that goes all the way down the ridge.

choices.text: Hum back, under the bell, every morning

effects.log: The bell rings, and the ridge rings with it, a second note under the first. Pilgrims come from the whole kingdom to hear the bell that the mountain answers. The abbot does not explain it. The abbot does not need to.

choices.text: Guard the temple quietly: fire, thieves, storms

effects.log: Twice the kitchens catch fire and twice a sudden rain puts them out. Once a band of thieves comes for the bell and leaves without their boots. The monks thank the Buddha. You do not mind at all.

choices.text: Listen to the monks chanting, year after year

effects.log: A sutra every dawn for years. You learn the Heart Sutra by heart without trying, all of it, and turn over its one idea for a decade: that the ridge and the dragon and the bell are all empty, and all real. It is a strange thing for a dragon to understand. It helps.

events.text: The palace stands under your shoulder. The court is a town of its own: three thousand mouths, ministers' mansions, a market, a prison. The levy for it falls on every village in the valley. And the king, who has heard rumours of a dragon in the ridge, wants it seen again, at the new year audience, before the envoys of three kingdoms.

choices.text: Rise at the audience. Let the envoys see

effects.log: You rise over the palace roofs at the new year audience in front of the envoys of three kingdoms. Three kingdoms go home and report that this king has a dragon. The king is very grateful. The levy goes up to pay for your shrine.

choices.text: Refuse. Lie still through the audience

effects.log: The audience waits. The king waits. Nothing happens. The envoys smile politely. The king is humiliated, and blames the court geomancer, who is exiled. You feel bad about the geomancer.

choices.text: Rise, but over the villages that pay the levy, not over the palace

ok.log: At the hour of the audience you rise over the poorest village in the valley, not the palace. The envoys see it from the terrace, and ask, pointedly, why the dragon shows itself over that village. The king, who is not stupid, halves the levy on it that spring.

fail.log: You rise over the village, but the court reports it as rising over the palace anyway, and the king is congratulated. Courts have their own ways of seeing.

events.text: Thirty years on, the temple builds a pagoda: nine storeys of wood, the tallest thing in the kingdom, one storey for each of the nine enemies at the borders, the abbot says, so that all nine will bow. It goes up against the sky beside your shoulder like a second ridge. From the top you can see the sea. The master carpenter, at the topping ceremony, swears the pagoda sways with the ridge, a little, in the wind.

choices.text: Hold the pagoda steady in every storm, for as long as you are here

effects.log: It never once falls in your time, though the storms that come off that sea could knock down a mountain. Far in the future it will burn in a war, and you, wherever you are then, will feel it.

choices.text: Coil around its foot on the night it is finished, so the monks remember

effects.log: In the morning the novices find the earth around the pagoda pressed into a great ring, scale-marked. The abbot has a wall built around the ring and calls it the dragon's seat. Pilgrims sit in it. You are flattered. You know you should not be.

events.text: There is a pool at the head of your valley, under the waterfall, so deep the bottom has never been found. One evening something comes up in it: a serpent, dark as old iron, as long as a ferry boat, with no horns at all. An Imugi. It looks at you, a dragon born a dragon, lying across the whole valley like a sleeping cat, and you see in its eyes a thousand years of not being one. "So," it says. "They just lay you in a well, do they."

choices.text: Bow your head to it. It has waited longer than you have lived

effects.log: The Imugi is so surprised that it sinks a little. "Nobody bows to a snake," it says at last. "Not even a dragon. Especially not a dragon." It watches you for the rest of the night, as if you were a riddle.

choices.text: Ask it how long it has been in your valley

effects.log: "Your valley," says the Imugi, and laughs, a sound like water going down a drain. "Four hundred years in this pool. Your valley. I like that. Go on, ridge. Tell me about your valley."

choices.text: Remind it whose valley this is

effects.log: The Imugi looks at you for a long time. "Yes," it says. "I have met dragons before. You all say that." It sinks out of sight without a ripple, and you lie there feeling, for no reason you can name, young.

events.text: The Imugi talks, on long nights, from the pool. It was born a water snake in a paddy ditch a thousand years ago. It has climbed every rung there is: the serpent, the great serpent, the thousand-year one. It has a pearl, now, the wish-pearl, found at the bottom of the sea after three hundred years of looking, and four claws to hold it. All it needs is to rise. And to rise, the old law says, the first one who sees it go up must call it a dragon.

choices.text: "Why does it matter what anyone calls you?"

effects.log: "Easy to ask, for something that was called a dragon in its egg," says the Imugi. Then, more quietly: "A name is the last thing heaven checks. I have done everything else. The name, I cannot do myself."

choices.text: Show it your fourth claw, so it knows you understand

effects.log: The Imugi looks at your claw for a long time, then at its own, which are scarred and very old. "Yours came in a hundred years," it says. "Mine took nine hundred." It does not sound bitter. It sounds tired.

choices.text: Tell it you were born a dragon, and that is not your fault

effects.log: "No," the Imugi agrees. "And it is not your doing either." It sinks. You lie awake the rest of the night, which for a ridge is a very long time.

events.text: The village is afraid of the pool. A calf went missing at the waterfall; a fisherman says he saw a black snake as long as a ferry. The headman leads a rite at the foot of your ridge with a pig's head and rice cakes, and the mudang, dancing, asks the dragon of the ridge to drive out the snake in the pool. They are asking you, quite specifically, by the name they have given you.

choices.text: Drive it out. The valley asked

effects.log: You come down on the pool like a landslide, and the Imugi goes, out through the falls and down the river to the sea, without fighting, without a word. The village is overjoyed. That night the pool is very empty, and so, in some way you cannot explain, are you.

choices.text: Refuse. Stay still through the rite

effects.log: The mudang dances all day. You do not move. The village decides the dragon and the snake are in league, and stops fishing the pool altogether, which suits the Imugi very well. "You owe me nothing," it says that night. "Thank you."

choices.text: Find the calf and bring it back to the village alive

ok.log: The calf is two valleys over, stuck in a bramble, very sorry for itself. You put it down in the middle of the rite. The mudang stops dancing. The headman looks at the calf, then at the ridge, then at the pool, and calls off the rite, and the snake is left in peace.

fail.log: The calf, it turns out, was eaten by a perfectly ordinary tiger. The village goes on being afraid of the pool. The Imugi does not seem to mind. It is used to it.

events.text: "At the spring equinox I will go up," the Imugi says. "I have the pearl. I have the claws. I have a thousand years. The first one to see me rise must say what I am, and I would rather it was not some fishwife with a basket on her head. I would rather it was you. Will you be my witness, dragon who was born?"

choices.text: Yes

effects.log: The Imugi does not thank you. It sinks to the bottom of the pool and stays there until the equinox, gathering itself, and you lie across the valley feeling the weight of a word you have not said yet.

choices.text: Ask why it trusts you

effects.log: "I do not," says the Imugi. "That is why it has to be you. If a dragon says snake, heaven will believe it. If a dragon says dragon, heaven will have to believe that too." It sinks. You are not sure that was an answer.

choices.text: Say you will be there. Do not say what you will say

effects.log: "That is fair," says the Imugi. "That is what a witness is." But it looks at you a long time before it sinks.

events.text: Spring equinox. The full moon. The pool boils white, and up out of it, through the falling water, comes the Imugi: iron-dark, four claws closed on a pearl that lights the whole valley green, rising, slowly, as if the air were deep water. The village is awake. Torches on the bank. A grandmother with a baby on her back. Everybody is looking at the serpent. The serpent is looking at you.

choices.text: "Dragon."

effects.log: You say it the only way you can, by rising beside it and bowing your head, ridge and all, so that the whole valley sees one dragon bow to another. On the bank the baby on the grandmother's back shouts "Dragon!", and the village takes it up, and the Imugi goes up through the rain of its own falls into the clouds, and there are horns on its head. There are two dragons in the valley's sky that night. Nobody who saw it ever forgets.

choices.text: "Snake."

effects.log: You turn your head away, the way you would from a snake in a ditch. The grandmother on the bank sees you do it and says, "It is only a snake." The Imugi stops in the air. It looks at you. Then it falls, a thousand years of it, into the pool, and the water comes over the bank and puts out every torch. In the dark you hear it say, very quietly, "I see."

choices.text: Say nothing. It is not your word to say

effects.log: You lie still. The Imugi hangs over the pool. Then the baby on the grandmother's back, who has never heard the old law and is not afraid of anything, points and shouts "Dragon!" and the serpent goes up, laughing, into the clouds, with horns. You had nothing to do with it. You are not sure whether that was the wisest thing you have ever done, or the most cowardly.

events.text: A storm comes over the ridge in a dry summer and stops over your valley, and in it, long and dark and horned, is the dragon you named. It rains on the village for three days, very gently, and on the third night it lies down on the saddle beside the Tiger's ridge for an hour, enormous, dripping. "I owe you a rain," it says. "I will pay it every hundred years. And when they ask you, up there, whether you were humble: I will tell them."

choices.text: Thank it, and ask it what the sky is like

effects.log: "Cold," it says. "Big. Full of dragons who were born dragons and think a thousand years in a pond is a story about somebody else." It looks at you. "Not all of them." It goes at dawn.

choices.text: Tell it you owe it nothing; it did its own climbing

effects.log: The new dragon laughs, a big sound now, like thunder rather than a drain. "That is why I owe you," it says, and goes up into its storm, and the valley has the best year of the century.

events.text: The pool under the falls has been still for ten years. Then one evening a dark head comes up in it, hornless, scarred, older. The Imugi did not die when it fell. It is waiting again, as the fallen ones do, for another thousand years, and it has chosen to wait in your valley, where you will see it every day.

choices.text: Go down to the pool and bow your head, as you should have

effects.log: The Imugi watches you bow for a long time. "Late," it says. "But not nothing." It sinks. Every spring after that, the first rain of the year falls on its pool first, and neither of you mentions it.

choices.text: Let it wait. You said what you saw

effects.log: It waits. You see it every day. Every day it looks at you. A ridge, you discover, cannot look away.

choices.text: Drive it out of your valley

effects.log: It goes without a fight, down the river to the sea. You have a clean valley and an empty pool. Somewhere in the deep a serpent tells the other serpents what kind of dragon you are.

events.text: Bandits in the north pass again: a dozen hungry men with spears and torches who come down every few years when the harvest is good, take what they can carry, and are gone by dawn. They are the valley's oldest trouble. Tonight they are driving three of the village's oxen up the pass, and a young farmer is running after them with a hoe.

choices.text: Close the pass in front of them

effects.log: A rockfall in front, the village behind. The bandits leave the oxen and scatter up the slopes like goats. The young farmer leads the oxen home in triumph and tells everyone the bandits ran from the hoe.

choices.text: Rise over the pass in the torchlight

effects.log: Twelve bandits look up at a head the size of a house with torchlight in its whiskers. Nobody has ever seen bandits move so fast. The oxen walk home by themselves.

choices.text: Catch the young farmer before the spears do, and let the oxen go

effects.log: A gust knocks the farmer flat into the bracken just as the spears turn. The oxen are gone. The farmer is alive. The village grumbles all winter about the oxen, which is exactly what a village should be grumbling about.

events.text: This time the bandits have a chief: {npc}, a deserter from the border garrison with a soldier's sword and a soldier's discipline, and forty men instead of twelve. They do not raid. They camp in the pass and send a message down to the village: a tenth of every harvest, every year, or they burn the valley. The headman has already started counting sacks.

choices.text: Bring the pass down on their camp in the night

mem.note: brought the mountain down on my camp

ok.log: The pass comes down like a closing door. Half the band is buried. {npc} digs out with a broken arm and leads the survivors over the far side of the mountain, looking back the whole way.

fail.log: The deserter has seen sieges. There are men with fire-arrows on the slope above, and pitch.
fail.deathCause: the fire-arrows of a deserter who had seen a siege

choices.text: Visit the chief's tent at night, and only look

mem.note: watched me through the tent flap

effects.log: {npc} wakes to a green eye at the tent flap the size of a shield, and lies very still, and does not reach for the sword, which tells you a great deal. In the morning the camp moves to the next valley. {npc} goes last, looking back.

choices.text: Make the valley harvest so big that a tenth is nothing, and watch

effects.log: The tenth is paid, and it is a great deal of grain, and the bandits eat well for a winter. Then they get lazy and comfortable, and {npc} comes down to the village one day to buy salt, like a neighbour. Strange things happen to bandits who are fed.

events.text: {npc} comes down the north pass alone, older, limping, with no sword. {He} stops at the foot of your ridge, where the villagers leave their offerings, kneels, and lays down a soldier's identity tag from the border garrison. "I deserted because they burned a village like this one," {he} says to the ridge. "Then I became them. I would like to stop. The headman says I can work the stony fields at the top of the valley, if the dragon does not object."

choices.text: Let a warm wind blow down the valley, from the ridge to {him}

mem.note: sent a warm wind when I knelt

effects.log: {npc} works the stony fields for years and is the first to the stockade when other bandits come, with a hoe and a soldier's eye. When {he} dies the village buries {him} by the north pass, facing out, on guard.

choices.text: Let the stony fields stay stony. Some debts are paid in sweat

mem.note: stony fields, and fair

effects.log: {npc} breaks {his} back on those fields for a decade, and gets a thin harvest, and does not complain. In the eleventh year you let the stones soften. {npc} notices, and bows, and says nothing.

choices.text: Send {him} away. The valley has long memories

mem.note: sent me away

effects.log: The wind turns cold and hard against {him}. {npc} picks up the tag and goes back up the pass. Nobody knows where to. The headman is relieved. The headman is also, privately, sorry.

events.text: Harvest moon, and smoke at the far end of the valley: raiders, and not hungry farmers this time but a mounted band from beyond the mountains, who burn what they cannot carry. The village bell is ringing. The stockade will not hold horses.

choices.text: Stand across the valley floor between the riders and the houses

ok.log: The horses will not face you. They rear and scream and throw their riders, and the raiders who keep their seats ride back the way they came. The village spends the rest of the night putting out the barns.

fail.log: Some of the horses are war-horses, and their riders have spears that know scales. You drive them off, at a price. (-16 health)

choices.text: Rain on the fires, and let the village defend itself

effects.log: A hard rain on the burning barns, and on the riders' torches, and on the bowstrings. The village fights at the stockade in the mud, and holds. They are prouder of that night than of anything you ever did for them, which is right.

choices.text: Lead the riders astray in a fog

ok.log: They ride into the fog and come out of it, at dawn, two valleys away and facing the wrong direction. They decide this valley is cursed. They are not entirely wrong.

fail.log: The fog confuses the villagers as much as the raiders. Two barns burn. (-2 ward)

events.text: Wood is spring, and spring is everything that grows. Fever grows too. It comes up the river road in the third month with a pedlar who coughs, and within a fortnight there are straw mats in every doorway of the village and a child burning hot on each one. You can feel it in the valley the way you feel a splinter: a small hot wrongness, spreading.

choices.text: Turn the wind, so it blows the fever back down the river road

ok.log: For forty days the wind blows down the valley and never up it, and the fever goes no further than the houses it is already in. Most of those children live. The village elders say it was the year the wind forgot how to turn.

fail.log: You turn the wind and the fever simply walks against it. Wind is not the way. Three children die before midsummer.

choices.text: Breathe green over the slopes, so every herb on the ridge comes up at once

effects.log: Mugwort, sweet flag, bellflower root, wild ginseng in the shade of the north face: all of it at once, in a week, more than anyone has seen in a lifetime. The village herb-woman climbs the ridge with a basket and comes down weeping. You feel thin for a season. (-8 health)

choices.text: Close the river road with a landslide

effects.log: The road is gone in a night. No more fever comes in. No more salt, cloth or news, either, until autumn, and a family trying to bring a sick grandmother home from the next village has to turn back. The valley lives. It is a hard way to live.

events.text: The herbs from the ridge are stronger than any the herb-woman has ever used: one leaf of your mugwort does the work of a handful. She grinds them in a stone mortar day and night and the fever starts to break, house by house. The village carves a new pair of guardian posts for the gate, with fierce painted faces, to keep out whatever comes next. And they come up the ridge, in a crowd, to bow.

choices.text: Let the herbs grow strong every spring from now on

effects.log: Every spring the ridge is a pharmacy. The herb-woman trains three apprentices. The village becomes known for medicine, and the sick come from two counties, and that, too, is a kind of ward.

choices.text: Stand up in the crowd's sight, so they know who to thank

effects.log: They know. They thank you, at length, every spring, with a rite and a table and a speech. The herb-woman, at the back, keeps grinding. You notice that she does not come to the rite.

choices.text: Let the herb-woman take the credit

effects.log: The herb-woman is the hero of the fever year. She did not sleep for forty nights; she deserves it. She knows where the herbs came from, though, and leaves a bowl of barley tea at the warm rock every spring until she dies.

events.text: Another spring, and another fever, and this one is not a sickness but a Guest. You can see it, coming up the river road on a white horse, in an official's hat, with a fan: Sonnim, the smallpox spirit, whom the people do not fight but host, with clean houses and quiet voices and food set out, so that it will pass through kindly. It stops at the village guardian posts at the gate and looks up at the ridge. It has manners. It is asking leave.

choices.text: Bow to the Guest, and ask it to pass through gently

ok.log: The Guest inclines its hat, and rides through the village at a walk, and touches every child lightly, and leaves before the new moon. The children are spotted for a month and then they are well. The mudang holds the sending-off rite on the river with a straw horse. The Guest, you think, was pleased.

fail.log: The Guest inclines its hat, politely, and rides through as it always rides. It is not cruel. It is not gentle either. Four small graves on the hillside that summer.

choices.text: Bar the road at the guardian posts

ok.log: You lie across the road at the gate, and the Guest on its white horse looks at you for a long time, and turns, and rides on up the valley to the next village instead. Your valley is spared. The next village is not. You had not thought about the next village.

fail.log: You cannot bar a Guest. It rides through you like mist and you shiver with fever for a season, and so does the village. (-12 health)

choices.text: Lay a feast of the ridge's best before it, and host it yourself

effects.log: Chestnuts, pine nuts, honey, the first bracken. The Guest dismounts and eats, which no one in the village has ever seen it do, and stays a long while talking, and when it rides through at last it rides very quickly, touching only a few. You run a fever for a month. A host takes some of the guest home. (-6 health)
